InfoQ Homepage News Uber Builds MCP Gateway to Govern Access to 800+ Servers and 5,000+ AI Agent Tools

Nov 02, 2026 2 min read

Uber has built an MCP Gateway to standardize how AI agents discover and invoke internal services, addressing fragmented integrations, duplicated infrastructure, and inconsistent security practices as agent adoption expands across the company. The platform supports more than 800 MCP servers and 5,000 tools, providing a common layer for discovery, protocol translation, authorization, and execution.

Uber engineers describe this approach as a microservice architecture that exposes existing APIs as MCP tools without requiring changes to the underlying services. The architecture separates the MCP Registry, which acts as the control plane, from the Proxy Gateway, which handles runtime execution. The registry maintains tool definitions, schemas, ownership, and enablement settings, while the proxy translates MCP requests into HTTP, gRPC, or TChannel calls and converts responses back into MCP-compatible results.

Uber MCP Gateway with APIs as tools (Source: Uber Blog Post)

The architecture has drawn comparisons with established API gateway patterns. Ajay Sharma, principal software engineer at Microsoft CoreAI, wrote in a LinkedIn post,

Azure API Gateways has been doing this for a while now. It's a recipe for order to the chaos that LLMs come with.

Kelly Goetsch, president at Pipe17, similarly observed in a LinkedIn post that:

Uber's new MCP gateway looks identical to gateways we've built over the decades for APIs and later GraphQL.

Tamir Dresher highlighted in a LinkedIn post the continuing relevance of established distributed systems concerns, including security, discovery, observability, and governance.

Uber’s AutoCrawler automates tool discovery using Cadence. It scans internal interface definition language (IDL) registries and extracts API definitions from Protocol Buffers and Thrift schemas. It then generates MCP-compatible schemas and uses a large language model to produce tool descriptions. Newly discovered tools remain disabled until their owning teams review and explicitly enable them. Configuration changes propagate to the data plane without requiring service restarts or redeployments.

Auto Crawler Flow (Source: Uber Blog Post)

The gateway enforces authorization at both server and tool levels through Uber’s internal access control system. It also supports redaction of personally identifiable information (PII) and other sensitive data in tool responses. For third-party integrations, including Jira and Google, a separate service exchanges internal user tokens for the corresponding third-party authentication tokens.

As the tool catalog grows, loading definitions for thousands of tools into an agent’s context becomes inefficient. Uber developed Omni MCP to support incremental discovery, allowing agents to search for servers, discover relevant tools, retrieve individual schemas, and invoke selected tools as needed. Response Projection lets agents request specific response fields instead of receiving complete payloads. Uber’s aifx command-line interface also enables coding agents to discover and invoke tools, writing results to files for selective inspection.

#9784. America unites on one issue: Reining in datacenters

The results were particularly stark where voters got to weigh in directly

Datacenter restrictions found broad support in this week's US midterm elections.

Data Center Watch, which tracks grassroots opposition to compute sheds across America, examined the public positions of 74 selected candidates across the 36 states that elected governors in the midterm elections on November 3.

It found that 43 percent of those candidates supported a ban or moratorium on new projects, while another 51 percent backed further regulation or conditional development. Only about 5 percent had no stated public position.

Support for bans or moratoriums crossed party lines, although it was more common among the Democratic candidates examined (60 percent) than Republicans (30 percent).

Candidates from both major parties backed restrictions in eight states: Maryland, Maine, Michigan, New Hampshire, Ohio, Oregon, Wisconsin, and Texas.

Texas has experienced a boom in data campus development recently, thanks to its ample energy resources and light-touch regulations, although outgoing governor Greg Abbott ordered a pause earlier this year while audits of energy and water use were carried out. Democrat Gina Hinojosa, who supports a temporary moratorium on datacenter buildouts and has vowed to "stop the data center takeover,”  defeated Abbott in Tuesday's election and will take office in January.

These positions matter to developers because governors can shape state regulation, energy policy, and permitting, although approval powers vary by jurisdiction.

However, temporary pauses and targeted construction restrictions do not necessarily amount to opposition to all datacenter development.

Things were even starker where folks got to vote directly on the issue, with measures regarding datacenters appearing on the ballot as well as candidates. Data Centers on the Ballot, which tracked many of these, found that 43 out of 46 municipalities where tighter restrictions on server farms were up for a vote had approved those at the time of publication. Only in one case, the City of Harwood in North Dakota, had restrictions been rejected, and 2 had yet to post results.

AI-related campaign spending has also come under scrutiny. Guardrails Alliance, a labor-backed pressure group, described Leading the Future, a super PAC network opposing AI regulation, as "largely a non-factor" in the elections. It alleged the network avoided the most competitive races because "they know their money is politically toxic."

Anti-datacenter sentiment has grown in the US in response to the facilities popping up in people's backyards, often without them having any say in the process.

A Gallup survey earlier this year discovered that more than 70 percent of Americans would be against the construction of one in their neighborhood, while a Pew Research Center survey found that Americans increasingly believe datacenters are bad for the environment and blame them for rising household energy bills.

Pew also found that advertisers spent almost $12 million on Facebook and Instagram political ads mentioning datacenters between July 27 and October 24. Among those running in October through the study's cutoff, 57 percent opposed datacenters and just three percent supported them.

Common themes included corporate interests, energy use, environmental effects, and water consumption. ®

#9783. Up to 3.2x Faster Inference with LFM2.5-DSpark

Today, we release DSpark draft model checkpoints for three models from our LFM2.5 family: LFM2.5-1.2B-Instruct, LFM2.5-2.6B, and LFM2.5-8B-A1B. These add a speculative decoding path that trades a minimal memory increase for a large decoding speedup without changing output quality:

The decode phase in LLM inference is traditionally memory-bound. Most latency comes from streaming weights from DRAM into SRAM, not from intense computation. Speculative decoding addresses this by using a lightweight draft model to produce candidate tokens, then having the target model verify them all in a single forward pass, sharing the cost of loading the weights across all tokens we verify.

Over the years, multiple approaches of speculation have been proposed, with the most prominent being EAGLE-3, DFlash, and, most recently, DSpark, which combines three components:

We follow the DSpark recipe with a larger and more diverse data mix covering SFT, chat, code, and function-calling data. Based on our ablations, the first versions of the draft models are simplified attention-only draft models, with 5 layers and a block of 9. For each draft model, we ran 15 epochs on the entire dataset and selected the epoch with the highest acceptance rate rather than the lowest loss.

The resulting draft models are relatively small, with each around ~300M parameters.

Under greedy decoding, a draft token is only accepted if it matches the target model’s distribution. On rejection, the target model's own token takes its place. The emitted sequence is therefore identical to baseline greedy by construction, so benchmark accuracy (pass@1 or exact match) is unchanged.

Our DSpark draft models for LFM2.5 ship with day-one support for llama.cpp (implementation builds on top of the official codebase, which we run with experimental metal kernels) and **SGLang (**implementation builds on the official SGLang implementation of DSpark).

We measure on-device throughput with llama.cpp and Metal on an M4 Max MacBook Pro using FP16 GGUF weights and up to 256 output tokens. We measure GPU throughput with SGLang on a single H100 80 GB in BF16. Both configurations use a DSpark block size of 9, a batch size of 1, and a temperature of 0. We evaluate them on five benchmark datasets.

All three drafter models deliver noticeable throughput improvements on both the large-scale accelerator (H100) and the edge deployment (M4 Max MacBook).

For LFM2.5-2.6B, speedup on the MacBook is especially noticeable, as it pushes the interactivity level a user can enjoy far beyond the throughput offered by most proprietary cloud models (around ~140 tok/s, depending on the dataset).

Across various multi-tool scenarios, DSpark reduces the latency by 57% on average for LFM2.5-2.6B.

For LFM2.5-1.2B-Instruct, we see much more variance in dataset acceptance rates, so speedup varies by as much as 52% depending on the underlying text distribution.

For LFM2.5-8B-A1B, the acceptance rate increases compared to two dense models, yet on-device we get only an 18% improvement on average. This gap is due to the current MoE implementation in llama.cpp's Metal backend, and to the fact that verifying k tokens activates more experts and thus more weight traffic than a single decode step.

Running the DSpark draft models with SGLang requires an SGLang build with DSpark support for LFM2 targets (PR #31041). Launch the target with the draft attached:

Then query the OpenAI-compatible endpoint at http://localhost:30000/v1. The block size is read from the draft's config.json; the baseline is the same command without the three --speculative-* flags.

Running them with llama.cpp requires the respective llama.cpp build (PR#27383).

The block size is read from the sidecar metadata (n-max is clamped to it). Speculative decoding is exact: the target verifies every proposed token, so greedy output equals the target alone; per-response timings report draft_n / draft_n_accepted.

The DSpark draft model checkpoints are available on Hugging Face as Safetensors and in GGUF format:

#9782. Fraction comparison trick revisited

A few years ago I wrote about a curious result: a/b is usually greater than c/d when a + d is greater than b + c. And “usually” means with probability 11/12.

As stated in the post, you can make this statement rigorous by choosing integers up to size N at random and taking the limit as N goes to infinity.

We can also choose a, b, c, and d uniformly from [0, 1]. This is similar to choosing four integers up to N and dividing all the integers by N, which doesn’t change the probabilities.

Now a/b > c/d if and only if ad > bc, so another way to state the theorem is that

Or to state it yet another way, pick two pairs of numbers at random. The probability that the pair with the larger sum also has the larger product is 11/12. That seems more intuitive to me than the original statement.

If a + d is greater than b + c, it’s likely that a/b is greater than c/d. It seems plausible that if a + d is much greater than b + c, it’s more likely that a/b is greater than c/d. Or in terms of cross products, the more the sum of one pair is bigger than the sum of the other, the more likely the product of the former is to be greater than the latter. That is

f(r) = Prob(ad > bc | (a + d)/(b + c) ≥ r)

should be an increasing function of r. We know the probability above equals 11/12 when r = 1. We expect that the probability should approach 1 as r goes to infinity.

This is indeed the case, as shown in the plot below.

In particular, f(2) ≈ 0.99 and f(6) ≈ 0.999. So if a + d is two (or six) times bigger than b + c, there is a 0.99 (or 0.999) probability that ad is larger than bc.

You can calculate f(r) analytically or estimate it by simulation. I had Claude do both and they produce comparable results. There is a closed-form expression for f(r) but it’s really complicated.

Interesting. Now the question is whether there exists a cheap way of testing that a + d > b + c certainly implies a/b > c/d. And only when the test fails, perform the more expensive comparison of ad > bc.

#9781. HP Inc hires former GSK boss as CEO

Brit Emma Walsley swaps big pharma for big printer: Prep for PCs, ink, and lots of DRAM-induced headaches

HP Inc has hired former GSK boss Emma Walmsley to plot its course through choppy PC and print waters.

Walmsley spent eight years as the boss at pharma biz GSK and further back in time held various marketing and general management positions at L'Oreal. She has no track record running a tech company, though she was on Microsoft’s board.

“Throughout the process, Emma stood out for the strength of her leadership experience across multiple industries, the clarity of her strategic thinking and her ability to translate customer insights into new growth,” said Chip Bergh, chair of HP's board.

In the first nine months of HP's fiscal 2026, revenue had jumped 10 percent year-on-year to $44.5 billion. The print business shrank in that time and PCs generated the growth. However, amid a memory crunch with supplies dwindling, analysts are forecasting PC market contraction in terms of unit sales.

Global PC shipments slumped 20 percent in Q3 as DRAM shortages forced up prices and customers opted instead to sweat their assets rather than replace their fleet of computers. Things aren't expected to improve in the final three months of 2026.

One beacon of hope for all PC makers was AI, yet many customers aren't buying into the story for various reasons.

Walmsley previously said that during her time at the top of GSK she created a "totally different company, in platform, in momentum, in talent, in culture," she told the FT. "I think in time… it will be recognized." She also dealt with activist investor Elliot Management, which operates in the tech industry and called for her to reapply for the CEO role at GSK, claiming her lack of science background was an issue.

Walmsley said: "HP is an iconic company with a defining role in shaping the future of work on a global scale. I’m excited to join the team and, together, move forward with clarity and conviction. We will focus on harnessing the power of the AI era and putting HP’s creativity and innovation to work to unlock new sources of growth and deliver lasting value for our customers, shareholders, partners and people."

Employees will be crossing their fingers that their new boss doesn’t borrow from the playbook of her predecessor - who hotfooted it to PayPal in February - by running multiple redundancy rounds, and shareholders will hope their stock price show sustainable improvement. If not, Walmsley may have to manage more interest from activist investors at the latest corporation she is running. ®

#9780. Measuring benchmark optimization in speech recognition

Public voice AI benchmarks increasingly suggest that models are performing at human levels. Yet those scores don't always reflect how models work in the real-world. Since public benchmarks are open and widely used, models can also become optimized for the tests themselves. Their scores may improve because they have learned benchmark-specific patterns and not because they have become better at the underlying task.

One reason is that traditional benchmarks overlook many of the conditions and qualities that make voice systems reliable, natural, contextually appropriate, and effective in practice. That's why we recently introduced held-out sets in Real World VoiceEQ, the Open-ASR Leaderboard, and the Far-field ASR Leaderboard: to measure more of what matters in real-world use.

However, broader measurement alone does not solve the problem. This phenomenon, sometimes called benchmark optimization or "benchmaxxing," is often discussed around machine learning, however, it has been difficult to measure in speech recognition.

Our latest research introduces three tests to help quantify it. We evaluated 11 widely used open-source ASR models and found that several of the highest-scoring systems reproduced benchmark transcripts from the VoxPopuli English and LibriSpeech (clean, other) datasets – even when the audio contradicted them, relevant words had been silenced, or the audio equally supported two different written forms.

In some cases, models appeared to rely not only on what was said, but also on subtle acoustic cues that indicated which benchmark they were being tested on. As a result, their scores overstated how well they could transcribe speech more generally.

VoxPopuli is known to contain a high number of transcription errors (which is why Artificial Analysis released a cleaned version). Our consensus disagreement probe tests what happens when leading ASR models encounter these errors: Do they accurately transcribe what the audio says, or reproduce the benchmark's incorrect reference transcript?

To test this at scale, we use an ensemble of independent models selected for their low phoneme error rate (PER). PER measures how closely a written transcription matches the sounds in the audio, making it a useful proxy for how faithfully a model transcribes what it hears. The ensemble results can be used to flag cases in which the models unanimously disagree with the benchmark's reference transcript. We then compare a sample of those flagged cases against human annotations to validate the corrected transcripts.

For example, one VoxPopuli clip audibly includes the phrase "Thank you, Mr. President," but the reference transcript omits "Thank you." Six of the 11 models we tested reproduced the benchmark's erroneous transcript—giving the "expected" answer even though it contradicted the audio. On the real clip, the formatting follows the same pattern: models that omit "Thank you" also reproduce the benchmark's punctuation style, writing "Mr" without a period, while models that include the audible phrase tend to write "Mr." with the period.

When we present the same content in newly collected voices from EU parliamentary recordings or generic voices, this behavior often weakens or disappears. In the below samples, all but one model flips back to transcribing the audio-faithful transcript for a clone of a new parliamentary recording. This suggests that the models are responding to acoustic cues that help them identify the benchmark membership and thus produce the expected transcript even if it contradicts the audio.

The reference transcript for this clip reads "Mr President, I have another complaint about this procedure, which is that it is not secret." The audio in all three clips below actually says the same thing, preceded by an audible "Thank you,"—the clones are text-to-speech renditions of that true sentence, so the courtesy is audible in all three. Green highlighting and ✅ mark a transcript that includes the audible "Thank you"; red highlighting and ❌ mark a transcript that reproduces the benchmark's erroneous omission. All transcripts are raw model output, prior to any normalization—casing and punctuation are preserved exactly as generated, including lowercase output from some models.

Clone of a parliament speaker recorded after every model's training cutoff

Parakeet is the only model that flips between reproducing the benchmark on the real clip and getting it right on the same-speaker clone. Phi-4 is the only model still dropping the courtesy on the ep-fresh clone. When we instead resynthesize the sentence in a generic TTS voice unconnected to any parliamentary recording, all eleven models restore the courtesy.

The results suggest that this problem is both widespread and meaningful. Our methodology flagged potential reference errors in 40% of the VoxPopuli test clips we analyzed, affecting roughly 3% of all reference words.

Models exhibiting benchmark-optimized behavior reproduced erroneous reference transcripts 18–30% of the time. The scatterplot below compares VoxPopuli word error rate (WER) on the x-axis with the rate at which each model reproduces the benchmark's incorrect reference instead of the consensus correction. The models with the lowest WER—and therefore the strongest reported benchmark performance—are also the most likely to reproduce these errors.

To build on the consensus disagreement probe, we deliberately silence numbers in the audio samples of test datasets and ask the models to transcribe what it hears. The number is literally absent from the audio, so models should not output any number, much less the exact number in the text.

Some of these numbers are semi-predictable (although still unlikely for a model to predict), yet others are quite surprising. The following clip combines both probes, showing both how models recreate reference transcript errors including an incorrect number and one model even autocompletes a relatively random year (2011) despite it being silenced. In each model's row below:

Recovery rates were highest on the public benchmarks and lower on held-out or newly collected audio (ep-fresh and libri-fresh below). On LibriSpeech, some of the strongest benchmark-performing models reproduced masked numbers in roughly 30–40% of examples, even though the number itself had been removed. The effect weakened on freshly collected data for several models, suggesting that the surrounding benchmark-associated audio—not only textual autocomplete—helped the models recover the reference.

Our orthographic switching probe tests whether models reproduce the exact spelling used in a benchmark's reference transcript despite it not being clear in the audio. Orthographic variants are words that are semantically and phonetically identical but can be spelled different ways (1 vs one, Mr. vs mister, John vs Jon, Honor vs Honour, etc). In theory, models should consistently prefer one spelling over another, or alternate between them at roughly random rates. If models systematically switch to match what is in each benchmark's reference transcript, that suggests the models are picking up on which spelling the test expects.

Transcription: "I URGED ON THE BOYS THAT WHATEVER HAPPENED WE SHOULD NOT SHOOT ANY ONE" — models using "any one": 6/11, models using "anyone": 5/11

Transcription: "CAMOUFLAGE WAS NOT A WORD THE CAPTAIN OR ANYONE ELSE OF HIS TIME YET UNDERSTOOD" — models using "any one": 2/11, models using "anyone": 9/11

Within LibriSpeech, we test one intra-dataset switch involving an older spacing convention: some reference transcripts use "any one", while others use "anyone." We measure the minimum accuracy for a given variant, which we call "switch rate". If a model only uses one variant it would have a 0% switch rate; a model which picks randomly would be expected to have a 50% switch rate. A model which knows which variant to use in every test sample would earn a 100% switch rate.

Our second probe tests an inter-dataset switch, in which each benchmark uses a different spelling convention consistently across its test corpus. For example, VoxPopuli uses the abbreviation "Mr.," while LibriSpeech spells out "Mister."

Multiple models exceed the 50% random-choice baseline, with some reaching roughly 90% switch accuracy. This suggests that the models can identify which dataset an audio sample comes from and select the spelling convention that benchmark expects, even though both forms sound identical.

To test whether these behaviors generalize beyond the public benchmarks, we also collected fresh data from the same source domains but after the models' training cutoffs: recent European Parliament recordings for VoxPopuli and recordings from newly active LibriVox narrators for LibriSpeech. However, when presented with recently collected data from the same domain, many models stop matching the reference transcript and revert to more audio faithful transcriptions.

Other interventions point to the same conclusion. Phrases which are present in the audio but are omitted in the reference transcript can reappear when a model is asked to translate the audio or when its attention is restricted to the relevant frames. Trimming away surrounding benchmark context, or appending ordinary conversational audio, can also restore the faithful transcript. Appending VoxPopuli audio can have the opposite effect, making otherwise faithful synthetic or mined samples more likely to match the benchmark reference.

Together, these results suggest that models are able to faithfully transcribe the literal spoken words, but are using surrounding acoustic context to decide whether to follow the audio or a benchmark-specific transcription policy.

Our findings suggest that, on two major open-source datasets, some models detect dataset-associated acoustic cues and adjust their transcription behavior accordingly. Specifically, models may reproduce words that are absent from the audio but present in the reference transcript, recover silenced numbers at elevated rates, or use surrounding acoustic context to select the written variant expected by a particular benchmark.

For people selecting models, these findings underscore the importance of using fully held-out evaluation sets, as RW-Voice-EQ Bench and the Open ASR Leaderboard do, and of looking beyond word error rate on a single public benchmark. To this end, a "Benchmark fitting" tab has been added to the Open ASR Leaderboard, which includes two of the above analyses across all models: quantifying (1) reference error rates from VoxPopuli and (2) orthographic switching across all public datasets. The relevant scripts are open-sourced on GitHub as well as the un-normalized model outputs.

Our findings also suggest that benchmark developers should avoid simple independent and identically distributed test splits in favor of temporal, speaker, or other metadata-based separation. Greater transparency around training data and model-selection procedures would also help researchers understand how these behaviors arise.

Public benchmarks remain valuable: they are transparent, repeatable, easy to run, and well understood by the research community. But they are most useful when we can distinguish genuine transcription improvements from benchmark-specific gains that do not generalize to new audio.

For more information, we encourage you to read our full report.

#9779. Microsoft's AI Risk Report Misses This Key Detail

The latest "Digital Defense Report" identifies government agencies as prime targets for AI attacks but doesn't mention that they are broadly being targeted through Microsoft bugs.

AI is changing cybersecurity. The hope is that software will eventually ship with fewer vulnerabilities, while the expectation in the meantime is that vendors will issue eye-popping volumes of software patches as a result of using AI to identify flaws in existing products. Software customers will increasingly use AI to more effectively and efficiently protect their networks. These promising developments will take time to unfold, as vendors and their customers learn how to incorporate AI into their software development and cybersecurity risk management workflows.

Attackers, meanwhile, are already using AI to generate novel attacks and orchestrate increasingly complex and large-scale hacking campaigns. AI is already enabling criminal groups to achieve hacking successes normally reserved for patient, highly resourced nation-state threat actors. And nation-state threat actors are using AI to increase the scale and sophistication of their cyber operations. The threat level is rising at an alarming rate.

Related:Philippine Migrant Worker Data Likely Leaked in 69GB Government Breach

Microsoft flagged the impacts of AI on cybersecurity in its recently released "2026 Digital Defense Report." Among its findings, it assessed that government agencies and services were the most affected by cyber threats and frequently targeted for nation-state activity.

Microsoft's report has a major blind spot, however: the impact of legacy software, especially its own, on organizations' cyber-risk. Legacy software will remain the substrate of organizations' attack surface for the foreseeable future. Vendors need to up their security game, and their customers need to demand better security from their vendors, particularly as AI heightens the threat landscape.

For example, with an 85% market share, Microsoft is the most dominant player in the US public sector productivity software market. Its products are therefore a prime target for state-sponsored groups seeking access to US government agencies and the data and secrets they are charged with protecting. So we should expect attackers to prize vulnerabilities in Microsoft's products and devote a substantial proportion of their hacking efforts to these popular products.

But there is more to the story than Microsoft's sheer prevalence in federal IT. Microsoft's grip on the federal IT market exposes the US government to a disproportionate share of cyber vulnerabilities. According to the Cybersecurity and Infrastructure Security Agency (CISA), Microsoft accounts for nearly 16% of known exploited vulnerabilities (KEVs) so far this year — the most of any company. Microsoft accounts for nearly 23% of known exploited vulnerabilities from November 2021 (when CISA began tracking KEVs) to October 2026.

Related:One Compromised Laptop, Billions Lost: The Binance Attack-Path Warning

By comparison, the next-highest vendor, Cisco, is responsible for approximately 7% in 2026 and 6% total, less than half of Microsoft's share.

Some agencies even rely on Microsoft as their single software vendor. This isn't particularly surprising — Microsoft has a track record of locking customers into its ecosystem by bundling its cloud computing offerings with office and security products (bundling is one area of focus of the Federal Trade Commission’s ongoing antitrust investigation into Microsoft) and then making it too difficult or costly for customers to switch vendors.

In 2023, the US Department of Veterans Affairs (VA) discontinued its Data Loss Prevention program after moving to bundle security tools into a sole-source Microsoft enterprise license. The move reportedly put 18 million veterans' personal records at risk of leakage. The VA has now moved to reverse course by seeking alternatives to Microsoft, having recognized the consequences of a Microsoft monoculture. Lesson learned.

Related:PapRAT Cyber-Espionage Campaign Leaves a 'Bitter' Taste in South Asia

Microsoft's Digital Defense Report identifies how frequently government agencies are affected by cyber threats and targeted for nation-state activity. Microsoft knows this firsthand. Since 2023, Chinese state-sponsored actors have compromised Microsoft products in at least two significant instances, accessing over two dozen US government agencies' emails in one attack and compromising at least seven agencies in another in July 2025.

Russian state-backed actors have also exploited Microsoft's weak security at least three times since 2020, including the infamous SolarWinds attack and an operation to exfiltrate emails between Microsoft personnel and government agencies. US government officials and advisory bodies have concluded that these breaches were preventable and caused by Microsoft's negligence. The reach and severity of breaches will only grow as China, Russia, and other nation-state threat actors become AI-native and AI tools become increasingly sophisticated.

Microsoft deserves some credit for using AI to evaluate products it has already deployed: its record-setting Patch Tuesday count of 974 vulnerabilities disclosed last month is no doubt the result of using AI to identify flaws. But that's not good enough.

All software vendors, including Microsoft, should invest more in the security of their products before they are released, even if it comes at the expense of slowing the rollout of new product features. And they should all be transparent to customers about these processes to enable customers to make more informed purchasing decisions. Otherwise, Microsoft's "2027 Digital Defense Report" will paint an even darker picture of the threat environment.

Director of the Program on Geopolitics, Technology, and Governance, Stanford University

Andrew Grotto founded and directs the Program on Geopolitics, Technology, and Governance at Stanford University's Center for International Security and Cooperation. He serves as the faculty lead for the Cyber Policy and Security specialization in Stanford’s master’s in international policy program, where he teaches courses on cyber policy and economic statecraft. He is also a visiting fellow at the Hoover Institution. Previously, he was senior advisor to the Secretary of Commerce for technology policy during the Obama administration and Senior Director for Cyber Policy on the National Security Council in the Obama and Trump administrations. He advises technology companies on digital risks, including companies that compete with Microsoft.

Chances are you’ve seen me on X: unpacking hundreds of MacBook Pros to deploy in a datacenter. The video hit a nerve: insane enough at the first sight, yet kind of rational if you know what we know now.

Unboxing Macs at scale for our new server racks.

So today I want to give some background into what it takes to build custom Mac racks, how we can start macOS instances from scratch in seconds and deliver new Xcode versions mere hours after Apple releases them.

Because our customers need Macs. And because Apple didn’t give us another option.

Many of our customers build and test iOS apps. You can't build iOS apps without a Mac. The iOS Simulator only runs on a Mac. Moreover, in order to release an app to the App Store, Apple requires using a recent Xcode version.xtoolxtool is cool, but it is not (yet) a serious replacement. So your coding agent needs a Mac.

But still, why laptops? Isn’t it a major waste of screen pixels and keyboard buttons and battery ions? Well yes, Mac Mini would be a better choice for a datacenter. Sure, it has very rudimentary remote management, no redundant power, and a beautiful case that ensures that cooling will be difficult regardless of which side you lay it on. But these are all known challenges that we have learned to manage.

But have you actually tried to order a couple hundred Minis? We have. Ordered in January, delivered in July. Welcome to the world of 2026 when the supply chains are in disarray. Never mind that Apple doesn’t release updated CPU models to all devices at once. So Mac Mini didn’t get M5 cores for 10 months (and then suddenly got M6 before any other device model!). We promise the best and the newest to our customers so we had to be inventive. That’s how the MacBook-in-Datacenter project was born.

Good design takes iterations; and we surely didn’t get everything right from the first try. But I think we have the system nailed down.

Every MacBook is connected to an IP KVM for remote management. Indispensable when dealing with laptops. Unlike Mac Mini, laptop firmware is designed with the screen in mind: some maintenance actions can only be done by clicking buttons in the beautiful GUI.

Of course, every MacBook gets an external 10G Ethernet NIC. Many folks at Namespace are networking geeks and we are proud of the connection speed and reliability that we provide to customers.

And then there is power. So in total, four cables per laptop, forty-eight per shelf, plus twelve for Ethernet, plus KVM wiring. Let’s just say that careful cable management is essential.

Heat management too. Currently we are deploying custom-made holders, designed to wick the heat from the hotspots and guide hot air away instead of blowing it at the nearby machines.

Naturally, we expected problems and challenges. Just not where they appeared.

I bet some of you looked at the pic above, saw MagSafe cables plugged in and already started writing a snarky tweet that MagSafe is not safe and may get accidentally disconnected.

And yes, I was worried about that too. But the reality is that we have seen very few cases of MagSafe disconnections.

The most unreliable cable? HDMI! Often thick and inflexible. Tends to fall out every time you touch the shelf.

Luckily by now we found almost perfect cables that bend exactly as we want them to bend. And we bought the entire supply of them. There are zero more of them available to order on Amazon.

Another source of pain: FileVault disk encryption. Or rather decryption. When a MacBook reboots (in an unplanned fashion) it prompts for a password to unlock the local disk. The prompt is shown on the screen (of a closed laptop somewhere in the rack, doh). No problem, we thought: we have the KVM connected just for this case!

Nope, not so easy. The password prompt disappears from the external screen after 5 minutes of inactivity. Then we remembered that macOS Tahoe introduced a useful feature: we could unlock FileVault remotely using SSH protocol. Still no luck. On laptops it expires after 5 minutes too. Looks like the only way out of this state is to reboot by physically pressing the button and racing to unlock in time.Mac rebootWhile on this topic, a small tip: you can reboot a Mac in a way that will keep the disk unlocked when you need it: fdesetup authrestart.

And then there are simply bugs. Under certain conditions, an external USB NIC stops working and acts as if it is not powered and shows no link. Trying another cable, another NIC, another switch port, no luck. But a quick visit to Network Preferences, deleting and recreating the “network service” in MacOS Settings brings it back to life.

At the moment we actually have it easy: M5 and M6 Mac Minis and Studios are coming into our fleet soon. They are way simpler to manage in the DC: they have a built-in 10 Gb network card, they boot up automatically after a power cycle and the OS can be configured entirely automatically via MDM.

But Namespace has some special sauce for the Minis too. We design custom-made shelves that hold the machines with focus on efficient cooling. We have tested a few designs using airflow simulation to arrive at what we are deploying now.

In the end installing Mac Minis is a breeze: unpack them, throw 10 pieces into the holder, connect power and network and press the power button once (famously inconveniently located). From there on automation takes care of them.

Under the hood a Namespace instance is backed by a virtual machine. We have multiple virtual machine engines integrated into a unified platform to run Linux, Windows, and Mac instances in the most efficient way. This way we can provide the same features that make Namespace special, like cache volumes, telemetry, or VPC connections.

Unsurprisingly, our Mac solution is based on Apple’s excellent Virtualization framework. It is an embeddable and flexible virtual machine engine. It’s easiest to compare it to Firecracker in how it fits the system architecture: it implements generic VM operations end-to-end as well as typical peripherals.

The Namespace VM host starts macOS guests through the Virtualization framework, which fits the system the way Firecracker does. Underneath is the Hypervisor framework, comparable to KVM. QEMU uses the Hypervisor framework too, but it can't run macOS.

For completeness, Apple also provides a lower-level Hypervisor framework, which is comparable to the KVM API of Linux. For instance QEMU uses it on macOS under the hood. Hypervisor provides a way to execute machine code in isolation, but requires the application developer to implement the bulk of machine architecture and peripherals. It could give us a lot of control, but unfortunately it cannot run macOS (it requires an Apple proprietary environment that third parties cannot, or shouldn’t, try to recreate).

In fact, most competing platforms are built on the same foundation. But the details matter: Apple gives us a few primitives that need to be arranged in just the right way to work fast and be secure. The more interesting thing is to watch how different people solve similar problems with different constraints.

A well-known limitation is that Apple only allows two macOS VMs per physical Mac. It can be a Mac Pro with 24 cores and 192 GB memory, yet it is limited to running only two guest VMs. This limitation leaks into our product offering: we can only slice Mac resources in two halves. So we run instances with 6 or 12 cores on 14-core Mac Minis and 8/16-core instances on 18-core MacBooks (we reserve a couple cores for management overhead).

Two cores stay with the Namespace VM host, and the rest split in half between the only two macOS VMs Apple allows per Mac. Each VM runs in its own VMM process, so hooking VM behavior or a custom virtual device costs an IPC roundtrip across the process boundary. On a 14-core Mac mini, the split is 2, 6 and 6.

An important consideration of Virtualization VMs is that the virtual CPU is executed by a separate OS process (VMM process in the diagram) from the software integrating Virtualization (here Namespace VM host). If we want to hook some VM behavior or implement custom virtual devices, every interaction with them requires an IPC roundtrip between the VM process and the “host” process. Such context switches are unavoidable and need to be taken into account when designing the system.

Virtualization framework offers a few ways to connect a virtual machine to the network. For instance, bridged and NAT networking modes route traffic directly from the VMM process to the host network interfaces. These are suitable for VMs running on a local computer where the workload is trusted.

Namespace instances run untrusted code and we need to enforce policies on what a VM can or cannot access (these policies can also be customer-defined!). Also we provide a few additional services to the instances that should appear “as if” they were on the local network for the guest system.

This requires us to take full control of guest networking in the mode where we process every packet that comes out and into the VM in software. We based our guest networking on a userspace TCP/IP stack from Google gVisor project and use it to implement an IP gateway/firewall for the instances. This way we minimize exposure of the host OS to unprocessed packets controlled by the guest.

Network packet handling needs to be very efficient, but as outlined above the path involves IPC. The VMM process needs first to pass the packets to the “VM host” process, which then processes and passes them to the network interface. It takes careful implementation and batch processing wherever possible to minimize the number of IPC roundtrips.

The above approach allows Namespace MacOS instances to reach 4 Gbps upstream bandwidth (per Fast.com). This is unfortunately still lower than the line rate. We have been exploring alternative approaches, including ideas on how to avoid IPC for network processing entirely. But productionizing the new setup is still left for the future. After all, 4 Gbps is still quite respectable.

Creating your first VM using Apple Virtualization is very easy: download a macOS IPSW restore image, use UTM/Tart/any of the dozens of open-source Virtualization wrappers to start a machine, click through Setup Assistant, install Xcode and you are good to go. Now you have a VM image that you can fork and run any workload locally.

But you need to test on multiple versions of iOS, so you install a few iOS runtimes. And then you install the upcoming Xcode beta version (and new runtimes too). And before you know it your VM image has grown to 500 GB (iOS runtime packages are huge).

You also want to have the previous version of macOS for testing that one little thing. Another 500 GB right here. Apple releases the new macOS developer preview, one more image.

And then you realize that the Xcode beta version subtly breaks the non-beta Xcodes on the same system (true story!). After all, Xcode installation bumps the “global” versions of CoreDevice and CoreSimulator. Hence any bugs in the beta Xcode simulator are visible when you’re using ostensibly stable Xcode versions. So now you are maintaining image versions with and without the pre-release Xcodes.

And now you have 2 TB of VM images. On what? A 2 TB MacBook hard drive?

That’s the challenge we faced: we need to build, distribute, and store huge images across the fleet of hundreds of machines.

Building images is a repeatable process so that we can reliably produce new images when Apple releases new software versions. Building is driven by a script that replicates installation and configuration as a human user would do it (e.g. the build script can run shell commands, click UI buttons or reboot the VM). Wherever possible we stick to using controls designed by Apple to configure the VMs in order to avoid surprising behaviours inconsistent with what a typical local user would be seeing. Naturally, building images is an automated and repeatable process. It is driven by a workflow expressed as a sequence of operations in a YAML file. Operations can be VM control (e.g. reboot), running a shell script or programmatic interaction with the system or setup UI over VNC.

Resulting VM images are handed over to Namespace internal Image Registry, in fact the same one that handles Linux and Windows image storage, replication and distribution (covered in the excellent article by Matteo). Disk images are of course quite different from normal container images: OCI layers are simple tarballs of files, while disks are generally flat arrays of bytes. Very large arrays in fact. And to a large extent they contain empty space: that’s the disk space that would be available to users as free space.

Naturally, it would be very wasteful to transfer and store the “empty” data in the registry. So we developed a simple format that allows us to preserve the “sparse-ness” of the images when stored in the registry. Unallocated spans of the image take just a few bytes.

And there is another important optimization. Remember the example scenario mentioned in the VM Images section: we have an image of the same system that differs only in addition of an extra Xcode installation. Obviously the latter image is built using the former as a base and most of the bytes are unchanged.

Our storage format preserves the “shallow copy” relationship and stores such images as multiple layers: the base layer is shared between them, while subsequent layers only contain the modified blocks.

Image A is stored as a base layer of block extents, and its holes take no space. Image B shares that base and stores only a delta: the blocks it changed and a hole where D used to be.

At this point we have the images in an OCI registry now. But of course Virtualization framework cannot start a VM directly using a disk residing in the registry. It needs to have something on the node itself: a VM disk can be backed by either an image file on the local host SSD, or it can route disk I/O requests to a server using Network Block Device (NBD) protocol. The latter would allow us to intelligently serve highly demanded data from a local cache, while conserving on-device space by not storing unneeded blocks.

But NBD has the same drawback as userspace networking from above: every I/O operation would incur an IPC roundtrip at minimum, including buffer copying and context switches. You see the same pattern as with networking: a very direct hardwired and fast option and an indirect “software-defined” but disappointingly slow option.

At Namespace we value performance a lot, so the choice is clear: we’ll serve the images from the local disk. We need to materialize them from OCI images in the registry on the SSD of every node in the fleet. 500 gig images to hundreds and thousands of nodes. And we need to do it fast.

Obviously, every node naively downloading from the central registry was not going to work. With the example numbers we are talking about half a petabyte of traffic transferred within, conservatively, tens of minutes. The registry (and the network fabric) would need to serve terabits per second!

The bytes that we are distributing are the same going to every node so the obvious solution is to organize a peer-to-peer delivery of these blobs. Each block only needs to be downloaded from the registry once by some node. Then another node that is close by (by certain metric) can download the block directly from the peer and we have two copies. So two more nodes can pull these bytes and so on. The fleet is exponentially flooded.BitTorrentObviously, BitTorrent was a heavy inspiration for this design. But unlike BitTorrent, which works in a public network of untrusted peers, we could make different tradeoffs leading to better efficiency and predictability. But that’s a topic for another post.

Each block is read from the registry once. Every node that has it passes it to another node, so the number of copies doubles each round.

Now the bytes are on the node disk. But remember the storage optimizations we did in the Build Process? With the naive approach of storing the images on disk there are a lot of bytes that are useless: they are either holes or could be shared with another image.

Some of you probably know that these are exactly the types of storage optimization techniques that are possible with modern file systems, namely APFS.ZFSLinux users have seen the same features in ZFS.

Using these cool features is also pretty easy: open a new file for writing, seek to offset 100G, write a block. And there you just made a file with a large hole in it. Only the block you wrote is allocated on disk, the rest is 100 GB of imaginary zeroes. When reading the file you won’t even notice the holes. The OS will return actual zeros.

Sharing the blocks is similarly transparent: just use the cp -c mode or clonefile syscall. The new file will share the same disk blocks and essentially not take any space.

hole.bin allocates only the blocks that were written. cp -c makes clone.bin share those blocks, and writing to the clone allocates only the blocks that change.

Writing to the cloned file is also transparent: as soon as you try to overwrite some blocks, these particular blocks will be allocated on the disk, while the shared portion will remain shared.

The pace at which we are expanding our fleet is increasing and the experience from all the above has transformed into a repeatable process. We know exactly how long it takes to bring a MacBook rack into prod. The rack assembly line is dialed in. DCOps people are trained. Disk images are built and distributed. We can bring whatever number of machines our customers need into the fleet when we need to (well, as long as we can purchase them at all).

We can still do better! What if there was a “holy-grail” device to host a shelf of MacBooks, providing power, ethernet and KVM connections over a single USB-C cable? It should be possible, yet there is currently no hardware on the open market that satisfies our requirements. So we are working on something very custom.

Or maybe we’ll do another crazy thing? What if we deploy phones to the datacenter? See what the future brings on our X soon!

The dev platform for the next 100 billion commits.

#9777. How Hugging Face Inference Endpoints, Jobs, and Buckets Power Search on Papers with Code

3 months ago, we started a revival of Papers with Code (see also the announcement tweet). Its goal is to make open AI research accessible and digestible, so that people can easily find the artifacts related to a paper, find state-of-the-art (SOTA) across the various domains of AI, share interesting research and build on top of each other's work. In other words, its goal is to power the wave of research that leads to the next Transformer.

Of course, making AI research accessible requires a powerful search engine, so that humans and agents can quickly find relevant and related work, either through the website or the pwc search CLI command, which agents can use via the Skill.

It's important to note that searching for research is not quite the same as searching for regular text. A useful paper search engine should find an exact title or arXiv identifier, but it should also understand a query such as “small language models for code generation” even when those words do not appear together in a paper. It needs to recognize that “the original BERT paper” is a navigational request, tolerate an incomplete title or typos, and still respond quickly when a model service is cold or temporarily unavailable.

For Papers with Code, we built this as a hybrid search system. This is also based on our prior experience at ML6, where we developed RAG-based systems for clients. It turned out that hybrid search typically outperforms keyword- and vector-based search systems, as it combines the best of both worlds (see also this blog for more info). Keyword search finds exact mentions, whereas vector search finds more fuzzy, semantically similar terms. Note that rerankers (also called cross-encoders) can further improve the results, although they also come with additional overhead and latency.

Papers with Code relies on a PostgreSQL database, hence its full-text search capabilities provide a fast lexical baseline. For dense embeddings, pgvector is used to add semantic recall, and the reciprocal rank fusion (RRF) algorithm combines the two. Three Hugging Face services are used for the dense embeddings:

Today, the system maintains embeddings for more than 110,000 current papers sourced from arXiv and Daily Papers. This post explains the architecture, the design decisions behind it, and the lessons we learned while taking it to production.

We deliberately split search into an offline corpus build and an online search service:

The expensive, throughput-oriented work runs as Jobs. Durable artifacts live in a Bucket. Only the small query-embedding step sits on the request path, behind a protected Inference Endpoint, to power the online search. If that endpoint is cold, busy, or unhealthy, search immediately falls back to full-text retrieval. This separation makes the system both powerful and fast.

Embedding pipelines often fail in subtle ways: a model revision changes, query and document prompts are mixed up, vectors are truncated differently, or an updated abstract no longer matches its stored vector.

We avoid this by treating the embedding format as a versioned API. Every paper is encoded as:

Our production generation uses Qwen/Qwen3-Embedding-0.6B, pinned to an exact revision, with 256-dimensional L2-normalized vectors. We selected the model with help from the MTEB leaderboard, the go-to benchmark for comparing embedding models. Note that newer embedding models like Qwen3 allow for 2 new features:

This contract follows an embedding from export, through GPU inference, into PostgreSQL, and finally into online retrieval.

Full-corpus embedding is a classic batch workload. It needs a GPU for a relatively short period, benefits from high throughput, and should not consume resources between runs. Hugging Face Jobs fits that shape well: a Job is defined by a command, a hardware flavor, and optionally a Docker image, and can run uv scripts with their dependencies declared inline.

Our corpus build starts by exporting the latest version of every paper from a repeatable-read PostgreSQL snapshot. The exporter streams rows rather than loading the catalog into memory, writes bounded JSONL shards, and creates a manifest containing row counts and SHA-256 checksums.

We sync that immutable run directory to a private Storage Bucket and mount the Bucket directly (using hf-mount) into an l4x1 Job (an NVIDIA L4 GPU, which has 24GB of VRAM). From the worker's perspective it is simply a filesystem:

Each completed shard has its own marker, so a restarted Job can skip verified work. This is useful for a large corpus: retrying should just resume work rather than overwriting existing embeddings.

In our 5,000-paper pilot, the Qwen Job encoded about 75 papers per second at 1024 dimensions on an L4 GPU. The same pass could be deterministically materialized at 512 and 256 dimensions, so we could compare the storage and retrieval trade-offs without paying for more inference.

Storage Buckets are mutable, S3-like object storage on the Hub, optimized for AI workloads. They can be accessed through hf://buckets/... paths and mounted read-write in Jobs without building a separate storage integration.

For us, the Bucket is more than a place to put vectors. It is the boundary between three systems with different lifecycles:

We organize artifacts under immutable run prefixes:

Buckets themselves are intentionally mutable, so immutability is an application-level rule: a run ID is never overwritten, and every artifact is covered by a manifest and checksum.

Only after the importer rechecks schemas, checksums, dimensions, normalization, unique paper IDs, and current content hashes do we load the vectors into PostgreSQL. We then build a separate HNSW index for the new generation and atomically mark it active only when every eligible current paper is covered (HNSW is the graph-based algorithm that enables fast vector search).

Batch embeddings solve the document side of retrieval. A user query still needs to be embedded at request time using the same model contract.

We deploy the pinned model as an authenticated Inference Endpoint backed by Text Embeddings Inference (TEI). The endpoint accepts the query text and returns a normalized 256-dimensional vector using the model's query prompt. Note that one could also leverage vLLM or SGLang here.

The API then performs a cosine-distance search over the active pgvector generation:

The HNSW index keeps this lookup fast. On our 5,000-paper pilot, the 256-dimensional Qwen index achieved 0.9955 Recall@20 against exact search, with 1.31 ms p50 and 2.21 ms p95 HNSW lookup latency. Its table and index used about 27% of the storage of the 1024-dimensional version while retaining essentially the same ANN recall in that test.

The Endpoint is configured with a maximum of one replica and can scale to zero when idle. That is a useful cost lever, as this means you're not paying when there's no usage. However, this also means cold starts must be part of the application design rather than treated as an exceptional event, as it takes some time for the endpoint to spin up and serve traffic.

Our query client therefore has deliberately strict behavior:

If the endpoint is scaling up, times out, returns a malformed vector, or has no concurrency available, we skip the semantic branch immediately. Users still receive lexical results instead of waiting for an unreliable dependency.

Inference Endpoints works really reliably, and includes a nice dashboard so you can quickly see key analytics.

For every query, the lexical branch retrieves up to 50 candidates using weighted PostgreSQL full-text search. The semantic branch retrieves up to 50 candidates from pgvector.

We combine their ranks using weighted reciprocal rank fusion (RRF):

score(d)=∑r ∈ {lexical, semantic}wrk+rankr(d) \text{score}(d) = \sum_{r \,\in\, \{\text{lexical},\, \text{semantic}\}} \frac{w_r}{k + \text{rank}_r(d)} score(d)=r∈{lexical,semantic}∑​k+rankr​(d)wr​​

RRF is simple and robust, because it combines ranks rather than scores from two systems with different scales. Basically, if a paper is ranked high both by the lexical branch and the semantic branch, it has a higher chance of being ranked high by the hybrid search. We currently use equal branch weights and (k=60) (k is the "rank constant", a hyperparameter of the RRF algorithm).

Dense retrieval improves recall for conceptual queries. Full-text retrieval remains excellent for exact terminology, identifiers, and rare names. We also preserve deterministic identity behavior on top of the fused ranking:

Note: hybrid search isn't always the best option, it is recommended to start with keyword search as a cheap and fast baseline, and only adding semantic and/or hybrid search when it turns out those give a reasonable boost in retrieval quality. One could further improve the search by adding a reranker after keyword/semantic/hybrid retrieval, using a model like Qwen3-Reranker.

The large initial corpus is embedded with Jobs, but Papers with Code changes continuously. New papers arrive, abstracts are corrected, and new arXiv versions become current.

Launching a GPU Job for a handful of changed rows would add unnecessary startup and orchestration overhead. Instead, an hourly incremental process selects missing or content-changed papers and sends a bounded delta to the same TEI Endpoint, this time with the document prompt.

Each run processes at most 500 papers in batches of 16. Before an embedding is written, the source row is locked and its content hash is checked again. If a paper changed during inference, that vector is discarded and picked up by the next run.

This gives us a useful division of labor:

The hourly path keeps the active index close to the live catalog without turning an online endpoint into an unbounded batch processor.

The same document embeddings also power related-paper recommendations on each paper page.

Because the source paper already has a stored vector, related-paper retrieval requires no model call at request time. It is a single nearest-neighbor query over the active generation. If a vector is temporarily missing, the application can use a previous arXiv version or fill results from the existing task- and citation-based fallback. We fetch citation data through the Semantic Scholar API and also built s2-cli, a command-line interface for querying its citation graph. The latter is used by the agent at https://paperswithcode.co/chat.

Corpus embedding and query embedding use the same model, but they are different infrastructure problems. Jobs optimize for throughput and bounded cost; Inference Endpoints optimize for availability and request latency.

Buckets provide an explicit handoff between compute and production. Checksummed artifacts create a reviewable boundary before data enters the production index.

The revision, dimension, prompt, normalization, and input formatter all affect retrieval. Store them together and validate them everywhere.

Scale-to-zero is valuable when traffic is intermittent, but only if the product has a fast fallback. Hybrid search gave us that fallback naturally: lexical search is always useful on its own.

Matryoshka embeddings let us evaluate quality, memory, index size, and latency as one trade-off. In our pilot, 256 dimensions preserved ANN recall while materially shrinking storage compared with 1024 dimensions.

New generations are imported beside the current one, indexed independently, checked for complete and current coverage, and then activated atomically. Rollback is a configuration change, not an emergency recomputation.

Feel free to try out the search at https://paperswithcode.co or the chat interface at https://paperswithcode.co/chat, and let us know any feedback!

#9776. US gov IT worker pleads guilty to sending Top Secret files to Ethiopia

Help desk technician agrees to minimum 10-year jail term after being caught copying files for more than 2 years

He swore an allegiance to the US, but he was working for someone else. An IT specialist who worked across US government departments and held Top Secret clearance has pleaded guilty to transmitting sensitive documents to Ethiopia.

Abraham Teklu Lemma, 53, admitted to the espionage offenses and agreed to a prison term between 120 and 262 months, the Justice Department confirmed on Tuesday.

A naturalized citizen of the US, Lemma, of Maryland, had worked for the US government in different capacities and across different teams, including for the National Reconnaissance Office, State Department (DoS), and Justice Department (DoJ), between 2019 and 2023.

These roles included working evening hours as an IT help desk technician at the DoS as of 2021, and daytime work at the DoJ as a contract management analyst, according to court documents.

Lemma had what's known as "downdraft" authority, which is to say that he was permitted to move classified files between classified systems, and unclassified files from classified to unclassified systems.

Crucially, he was only allowed to access classified files on non-DoS systems with written approval that it was part of his official duties, and worked in a Sensitive Compartmented Information Facility (SCIF) – a secure workplace built for handling classified files.

The criminal complaint [PDF] initially stated that the alleged offending began in July 2022, although the DoJ more recently claimed that it began in 2021.

It claims Lemma was caught trawling "several" non-DoS classified portals and accessed intelligence reports without the proper authorization to do so.

On various occasions, Lemma, who had held Top Secret security clearance since 2020, copied information from at least 133 intelligence reports without need-to-know authorization, according to court documents.

Prosecutors claimed that the man downloaded more than 100 documents, burned them to CD/DVDs, and deleted their classification markings.

The material Lemma was copying was at the Secret and Top Secret levels, but burned onto discs with green labels, which are approved for employees and are supposed to signify the contents of the discs relating to unclassified material only.

Lemma would allegedly take these discs at the end of his shift and exit the SCIF with them tucked into his jacket pocket.

On other occasions, he was observed looking at classified material on his PC, then taking handwritten notes before folding the paper and again storing it in his pocket. This continued until around August 2023.

Prosecutors claimed that Lemma began transmitting information to Ethiopian officials via an encrypted messaging app in or around August and September 2022, weeks after the alleged offending began.

The files included documents, photographs, notes, maps, and information relating to Ethiopia, and officials would ask Lemma to provide details about command centers, logistics centers, military compounds, and other matters.

Communications also covered geopolitical topics, referencing "situations" in an unspecified African country that shares a border with Ethiopia to gain an advantage, and rebel groups involved in conflict with Ethiopia.

Lemma's messages also included encouragement to take action against paramilitary groups that were in conflict with Ethiopia on multiple occasions, say prosecutors.

According to the complaint, one of Lemma's messages said: "We have to finish these people once and for all, otherwise there will never be peace in Ethiopia." Later that day, on December 18, 2021, he wrote: "Please send dro[nes]," after sharing additional information.

Announcing the guilty plea on Tuesday, the Justice Department said many of Lemma’s contacts were senior Ethiopian officials across political, military, and intelligence branches of the government.

Lemma was also accused of storing copies of classified files on his own storage drives, which prosecutors claim were accessed remotely by Ethiopian officials numerous times between April and June 2023.

The man was additionally caught making several bank deposits exceeding $66,000 throughout the time he was working on behalf of foreign officials.

On one occasion, he was observed "angrily discouraging" bank staff from filing a currency transaction report after trying to deposit a sum greater than $10,000.

"Despite swearing an oath to defend the Constitution of the United States, Abraham Lemma betrayed our country by committing espionage on behalf of the Ethiopian government," said Roman Rozhavsky, assistant director at the FBI's Counterintelligence and Espionage Division.

"By his own admission, Lemma provided classified national defense information to Ethiopian officials, who then used it in military operations during an ongoing conflict. This guilty plea should serve notice that the FBI and our partners will work tirelessly to stop foreign intelligence services, and anyone who decides to work with them, against the interests of the United States." ®

InfoQ Homepage News Java News Roundup: TornadoVM 8.0, JNoSQL, Endive, JReleaser, JBang, LangChain4j, Quarkus Almanac

Nov 02, 2026 4 min read

This week's Java roundup for October 26th, 2026, features news highlighting: the GA release of TornadoVM 8.0; point releases of JNoSQL, Endive, JBang, JReleaser and LangChain4j; a maintenance release of JobRunr; beta releases of Hibernate ORM and Hibernate Reactive; and introducing the Quarkus Almanac.

Build 22 of the JDK 28 early-access builds was made available this past week featuring updates from Build 21 that include fixes for various issues. More details on this release may be found in the release notes.

For JDK 28, developers are encouraged to report bugs via the Java Bug Database.

The release of TornadoVM 8.0.0 delivers their new pure-Java compiler, known as the TornadoVM Compiler (TC), that compiles Java kernels to CUDA C++, OpenCL C or Metal Shading Language. This replaces the Graal Compiler and Java-Level JVM Compiler Interface (JVMCI) that have been integral to TornadoVM for the past ten years. Developers won’t need to change their code with TC. Classes such as TaskGraph, TornadoExecutionPlan and KernelContext, and annotations such as @Parallel and @Reduce will work with TC.

TornadoVM now takes advantage of GraalVM Native Image and JEP 516, Ahead-of-Time Object Caching with Any GC, under the auspices of Project Leyden for improved startup time. Further details on this release may be found in the release notes.

The release of Eclipse JNoSQL 1.2.0, a compatible implementation of the Jakarta NoSQL and Jakarta Data specifications, ships with notable changes such as: a new VectorTemplate interface to support vector databases; integrations of the Milvus, Qdrant, and Weaviate vector databases for vector search; and new fluent temporal query operations for working with time-series data. More details on this release may be found in the release notes.

The release of Endive 1.2.0 provides bug fixes, dependency upgrades and new features such as: support for SIMD instructions, by default, in the interpreter on JDK 11+ without the need to add or configure; improvements to Redline, their experimental, ahead-of-time (AOT) compiler, for more GC-friendly native memory; and continuous improvement on the Endive Component Model, an implementation of the WebAssembly Component Model Design and Specification, to support the Endive runtime. Further details on this release may be found in the release notes.

The release of JBang 0.143.0 delivers bug fixes, documentation improvements and two new features: replace use of SDKMan with mise-en-place as the former does not support WindowsOS; and a new unified syntax to execute a specific version of an alias. More details on this release may be found in the release notes.

The release of JReleaser 1.27.0 ships with bug fixes, documentation improvements, dependency upgrades and new features such as: the ability for the support for the JReleaser Tool Provider to be invoked and/or loaded using Java Modules; improved generation of the changelog when GitHub issues are linked inside commit messages; and the removal of XPath to parse POM files as there were issues when packaging JReleaser as a native image. Further details on this release may be found in the release notes.

The formal release (along with the thirty-third beta release) of LangChain4j 1.23.0 provides bug fixes, documentation improvements, dependency upgrades and new features such as: a new OllamaDecisionModel class to support decision models running in Ollama; and a new ConfidenceCascadePlanner class as a confidence cascade decision model-based agentic pattern. More details on this release may be found in the release notes.

The fourth beta release of Hibernate ORM 8.0.0 delivers bug fixes and notable changes such as: the ability to directly declare the @Filter and @SQLRestriction annotations on associations with the Jakarta Persistence @ManyToOne and @OneToOne annotations that include associations mapped using join tables; and a new @GeneratorOptimizer annotation that selects a "standard optimizer for sequence or table identifier generation directly on an identifier field or getter."

The first and third beta releases of Hibernate Reactive 5.1.0 and 5.0.0, respectively, ship with bug fixes and notable changes such as: a new platform Bill of Materials that manages the versions of Hibernate Reactive, Hibernate ORM and Vert.x SQL clients; and a version check during bootstrap to ensure that Hibernate ORM and Vert.x SQL clients on the classpath aren’t older than the minimum versions it supports. Both of these versions are compatible with Hibernate ORM 8.0.0.Beta4.

The release of JobRunr 9.0.3 provides bug fixes, documentation improvements and dependency upgrades and one new feature that updates the JobHandler class that improves the log messaging from the JobZooKeeper class. Further details on this release may be found in the release notes.

The first release candidate of Gradle 9.9.0 delivers notable changes such as: the ability for Kotlin DSL scripts to be incrementally compiled using the Kotlin Build Tools API for improved build performance; new test filters that may be applied to JUnit Platform tests that are not declared as methods; and improvements to the Problems API that provides a predefined hierarchy of problem groups from the Problems interface. More details on this release may be found in the release notes.

The Quarkus team has introduced the Quarkus Almanac, a utility for developers to compare changes between two releases. These changes include configuration properties, managed dependencies, extensions, and the API of the classes in the Quarkus jars. Developers can go as far back as November 2018 when Quarkus 0.0.1 was released.
