#9698. The model that didn't exist, so you made it yourself

Last week, I wanted a small version of the prompt rewriter that ships with Qwen-Image 2.1. The official one is a 9B model that needs about 20 GB of memory and thinks for thousands of tokens before writing a single paragraph. On the Hub, I found only compressed copies of that same 9B model. So I described what I wanted to ML Intern, and the next day I had a 0.8B version that runs on a CPU. It returns valid output 99.7% of the time and uses about a quarter of the teacher's tokens. The compute for the whole project, including having the 9B model label 8,797 example requests, came to USD 16.

Over the course of the next few days, I made five more models the same way. Each one started as a message in HuggingChat with ML-intern switched on, and each one ended as a public model on the Hub with its evaluation in the model card. ML-intern plans the work, asks me for a budget before it spends anything, runs a small test before the real job, then trains, evaluates and publishes on Hugging Face hardware.

The first message is where I spend my effort. My first prompt, for the citrus model shared below, was about 450 words. By my 6th project it was closer to 2,000, because each project taught me something I wanted in the next one. All seven prompts are on GitHub at yvrjsharma/ml-intern-prompts, exactly as I wrote them.

A prompt starts with the idea in one line and why I want it. Then it names the exact pieces: the dataset, the base model, the training script. Anything I have already checked goes under a heading that literally says "Verified facts, do not re-derive", so the agent spends its budget on the work instead of rediscovering what I know. For the camera-angle LoRA that section listed which trainer had just added transparent-image support, and which open GitHub issues made the fallback trainer risky.

Two lines in the prompt are critical. The first asks for a baseline before any training. For example, the citrus prompt says: "Also report the base model's zero-shot score on the same metric before training so we can see the gain." Without it you get a trained model and no idea whether it is better than what you started with. The second is a smoke test with a check attached. For the image LoRAs I asked for 50 training steps, then a check that the saved weights had actually changed, before paying for the full run.

At the end of the prompt, I lay out the expected deliverables and limit the cost. I define what belongs in the model card and include a instruction like: "Cap total spend at USD 12 and ask me before exceeding it." Because ML-intern begins every task with zero dollar budget and needs permission before executing paid jobs, this spending limit stays strictly enforced. When you leave out a budget, the agent suggests a couple of paths depending on project size and asks which one you prefer.

You don't necessarily need all of that on your first attempt. For example, I didn't have the verified-facts section in my citrus brief and ML Intern still produced a model that more than tripled the accuracy of the Qwen3.5-2B model. Let me walk you through 6 things I built with Ml-Intern in just a couple of days.

A general vision model can describe a yellowing citrus leaf. However, telling you whether it is a mite problem or a magnesium deficiency, and the bio and non-bio remedies to treat the plant is very hard. Using Claude, I put together a training dataset merged from three sources hosted by the Project-AgML organization on the Hub. The resulting citrus-disease-vlm-instruct is a dataset containing 3,017 annotated images across 21 distinct pests, illnesses, nutritional gaps, and treatment approaches. ML-intern handled the fine-tuning of Qwen3.5-2B using these examples, making sure to benchmark the foundation model beforehand.

On the 335 test photos, the base model named the right problem 14.9% of the time. After two epochs on one A10G, the fine-tuned model got 52.8%. Compute cost, about USD 1.90.

Check out: Model · Dataset · Citrus Doctor App

Image models know plenty of characters. Huggy, drawn in the flat style of the Hugging Face brand assets, was not one of them. I asked ML-Intern for a LoRA on FLUX.2 klein base 4B, trained on 84 captioned drawings from Chunte/huggy_for_training dataset.

The agent saved a checkpoint every 100 steps and drew the same set of prompts with each one, which made choosing easy. Step 200 was the first where Huggy was fully on-model. From step 500 on, Huggy's style started bleeding into prompts that had nothing to do with Huggy! The trained LoRA also works on the distilled klein model at 4 steps. Compute cost, about USD 7.60.

Check out: Model · Dataset · Huggy Generator App

ML-intern rendered 1,030 scanned household objects from Google Scanned Objects at 24 angles each, 24,722 transparent images, on a CPU job that cost a few cents. It later finalised 461 objects for training and 40 held out for testing, and 1,844 before-and-after training pairs spread evenly over 23 camera instructions.

Training ran 2,000 steps in about 90 minutes on one A100 (~USD 3.75). The whole project took about half a day and 48 jobs, counting the ones that failed on missing packages or wrong paths and had to be resubmitted by ML-Intern. Total compute cost, about USD 16.

Check out: Model · Dataset · Viewpoint Orbit App

No dataset existed for this, so my prompt described how to make one. Start from a real photo in Open Images, remove one object with the LaMa inpainting model, and draw a scribble where the object used to be. The untouched photo is the target. ML-intern wrote and tested the pair-building scripts in a CPU sandbox, then ran them as GPU jobs, recording the author and license of every source photo along the way. It built 6,042 training pairs and a 160-pair test set, where 40 of the test pairs come from 23 object classes kept out of training entirely.

Before training, it measured the base model on its own and with the Viggle turbo LoRA, and checked that running edits in batches produced identical images, which made the evaluation cheaper. Training ran 2,000 steps in 1 hour 38 minutes on one A100 (~USD 4), and a comparison of the saved checkpoints on 48 test pairs picked step 500.

Paired with the Viggle turbo LoRA at 6 steps the LoRA performed really well. 67.5% of objects detected where they were drawn, at 4.7 seconds per edit. Objects from the 23 unseen classes landed as reliably as the rest (65.0% versus 64.2%). The project took a little over a day and 59 jobs. Total compute cost, about USD 24.

Check out: Model · Dataset · Doodle-in App

Training the 0.8B and 2B students took 12 and 18 minutes on an A10G (USD 0.75 for both). The 0.8B also ships as an 812 MB GGUF file for running on a CPU. The project took about 11 hours and 24 jobs. Total compute cost, about USD 16.

Check out: Pocket rewriter 0.8B Student · 2B Student · Dataset · Pocket Studio App · Compare the teacher-student in Rewriter Arena

It took two runs. The first cached 155,000 training images as latents, baked the guidance into the model, then cut the step count in stages from 16 to 8 to 4, all on A100s. The 4-step student beat the teacher run at the same 4 steps on GenEval and FID, after that ML-intern exported it to ONNX for the browser. This run took about 13 hours and USD 22.

I did a second training run by asking ML-Intern to improve the 4-step student a bit more. It then made 24,000 more image pairs with the teacher at 16 steps and fine-tuned the 4-step student against them for about an hour. GenEval went from 0.509 to 0.536, against the teacher's 0.563 at 50 steps, with just 4 steps (one-fourth the compute). ML-intern re-exported the browser version. The second run took about 8 hours. Total compute cost across both runs, about USD 37.

Check out: Agate 4-step model · Dataset · Run Agate in your browser · Agate 4-step LIVE

These are the GPU and CPU job charges reported for each session.

ML-intern is in HuggingChat. Switch on ML-intern mode and paste a prompt. If you want a starting point, my example prompts are free to copy. Start from a model you wish existed and a dataset you have, or one you can describe. Give it a small budget, ask for a baseline and a smoke test, and read what comes back before you raise the cap.

If you make something with it, share it on X and tag @Gradio and @HuggingFace. We would love to see the models you make that nobody else would think to build for you.

#9697. C++26 Disapproved

On October 23, 2026, the unthinkable happened. It was supposed to be a mere formality: C++26 was up for a vote by the ISO National Bodies (NBs). The options are always approval, rejection, or abstention. Comments are also allowed. Since 1998, this process had run quietly and smoothly. Not so on October 23, 2026. After a twelve-week voting period, the result is in: Disapproved!

I would like to mention here that I am a member of the C++ Standardization Committee and, together with my colleagues, represent Germany’s vote. ISO rules also stipulate that certain votes are internal to ISO, and the results—or the breakdown of the results—may not be published. This article contains my own personal views.

As far as I know, this is the first time in the history of C++ that DIS ballot failed. When I searched the ISO system, I could only find one other DIS that was not approved: ISO/IEC DIS 26926 C++/CLI Language Specification dated August 11, 2006. It’s possible that my search privileges aren’t sufficient to view everything, but all ISO programming languages should be visible to me. The sad end of ISO/IEC DIS 26926: the project was halted. I mention this upfront to clarify the significance of this vote.

In the following, I will use various terms from everyday ISO terminology. At https://isocpp.org/std/iso-iec-jtc1-procedures, there is an overview of the various stages of an ISO standard. DIS is the penultimate stage. As the overview also shows, a two-thirds majority is required. This majority was not achieved.

The reason for the rejection is quite clear from the comments submitted by the National Bodies (NBs): contracts. Put simply, a number of NBs believe that this feature is not yet ready for release.

Now it gets complicated. The C++ Standardization Committee, also known as WG21, follows ISO rules but also has some additional rules. One of these is (or was) that opinions are always heard whenever new information becomes available. If an opinion was heard and a feature was nevertheless not changed as desired, the person respects the outcome and accepts that many others disagree.

However, the voting body at the NB level may also consist of other individuals, or the NBs are, of course, free to vote differently.

The previous practice was that NBs would only vote against a standard if new information became available or if errors in the process or similar issues were identified. This changed on October 23, 2026.

It’s difficult to judge in this complex situation; the NBs who want C++26 without Contracts argue that there is new information. I myself find it hard to share this view. A new paper with old arguments is not new information to me.

The feature has been on the wish list for a long time. I was already in the room in Cologne back in 2019, at the time for C++20, when Contracts, in a different form back then, were being included in the standard. I was also in the room when the feature was removed from C++20 again during the same meeting. As a result, a study group was formed to address the topic of Contracts and its various aspects from 2020 to approximately 2024. Afterward, the study group submitted its work and proposals to the Evolution Working Group (EWG), the central body for language extensions. There, the topic was discussed further over several meetings before being included in C++26 by a majority vote.

In the next step, WG21 voted on the C++26 draft in March 2026, which included Contracts. Here, too, a large majority was achieved, though not without dissenting votes.

And that brings us to the next phase: DIS. At this stage, there were enough “no” votes that a two-thirds majority was not reached.

The big problem: what happens next? ISO, of course, has a process for this. It offers various options:

All of these possibilities mean a delay in the next C++ standard. Whether it will still be called C++26 is also up in the air, but that’s a much smaller issue.

The difficulty with all four options is that they require a majority within WG21. However, this working group voted to move C++26 with Contracts into the next voting phase leading to its release. And it did so with more than just the required two-thirds majority. The feature didn’t come out of nowhere, either; it was developed over the course of years through the work and possibly personal commitment of many people. It’s hard to imagine that this group would simply want to abandon its work, which has received approval on multiple occasions so far. The same applies to the group that is dissatisfied with Contracts. This group, too, has invested effort, in some cases even in alternative implementations. It’s hard to imagine that, after these groups voted “no” in the DIS vote, the result would change without Contracts being removed.

Even the last option removing C++26 requires a majority in WG21. As I understand it, this step would mean reverting to C++23 and proceeding to C++29 without a single change. This would affect the work of even more people. WG21 would then be tasked with incorporating features that have already been successfully included in C++26 into C++29. Since this can only be done through a paper backed by at least one person advocating for it, features could be omitted if that person lacks the motivation or time.

Of course, certainty about the voting outcome can only be achieved if the respective path is actually taken.

Unfortunately, the way forward is currently more than uncertain. Perhaps this also explains why ISO/IEC DIS 26926 marked the end of this activity. Consensus is needed to move forward. Trust is always required for consensus. Unfortunately, that trust has just been shaken.

The next C++ standard, and thus the future of C++, is currently at an impasse.

The good news is that the next meeting will take place on November 16, which is just a few days away. The top priority will be to break the deadlock. This will very likely have implications for C++29 as well; in fact, there is currently no reason to continue working on this project.

Normally, my articles are technically focused and free of personal opinion. Regarding the rejected DIS, I can only say that I consider it a massive disaster and feel sorry for the entire C++ community. Regardless of whether someone likes Contracts, considers them important, or sees major weaknesses in them, the topic has been worked on for years and has received a majority vote multiple times in its current form. By voting “no,” an established system, one based primarily on trust and respectful collaboration, has been shaken. Every ISO standard is simply a set of compromises. Everyone loses sometimes, and everyone wins sometimes. Overall, the result is one in which all participants have given their best. During the DIS vote, the losing parties refused to accept their loss. The question that primarily determines how to move forward is whether the group can rebuild trust.

#9695. Run fast, private agents on-device with LFM2.5-24B-A2B

LFM2.5-24B-A2B is a 24B-parameter reasoning model with just 2B active parameters, built for fast, private agents on-device. It thinks before it answers, calls tools, and works through multi-step tasks inside popular agent harnesses. Because only 2B parameters are active per token, each reasoning token is cheap, so you can run agents continuously on your own hardware.

LFM2.5-24B-A2B builds on LFM2-24B-A2B and keeps its architecture: 40 layers, 64 experts per MoE block with top-4 routing, and the same hybrid of gated short convolutions and GQA. The context window grows from 32K to 131K tokens, and an in-place tokenizer expansion doubles the vocabulary from 65K to 128K tokens for better non-Latin tokenization. Unlike its predecessor, it is a reasoning-only model that produces an explicit chain of thought before its final answer.

Pre-training was scaled up from ~17T to ~33T tokens. Mid-training then adds 2T tokens at 32K context, weighted toward reasoning, math, code, instruction following, and multilingual text, and 300B tokens at 131K context, weighted toward long-context data. Tool calls and multi-turn trajectories appear throughout both phases. Post-training turns the base model into an agent in five stages:

We evaluated LFM2.5-24B-A2B against Qwen3.6-35B-A3B, Gemma-4-26B-A4B-it, and Nemotron-3.5-Lightning on 16 benchmarks covering tool use and agentic workflows, knowledge, instruction following, math, and coding. It is the smallest model in the group, yet it is competitive with MoEs with ~50% more total and active parameters.

*All the models were evaluated with vLLM, using each benchmark's recommended generation parameters.

For your app, the strengths are tool use and instruction following. LFM2.5-24B-A2B leads or matches the competition on five of the eight tool-use and agentic benchmarks (AutomationBench, BFCLv4, ToolSandbox, LiveClaw, and τ³-Bench Banking), and on AutomationBench it scores more than three times the next-best model. It also leads on all three instruction-following benchmarks. Larger models keep an edge on knowledge-heavy benchmarks like GPQA Diamond, HLE, and AA-Omniscience, and on coding benchmarks like SWE-Bench Verified (OpenCode) and SciCode, so pair LFM2.5-24B-A2B with retrieval or web search for knowledge-heavy workloads.

These results make LFM2.5-24B-A2B a strong foundation for agents that need to reason, call tools, and run reliably on your device.

LFM2.5-24B-A2B ships with day-one support across the inference ecosystem, including llama.cpp, MLX, vLLM, SGLang, and ONNX.

Edge inference. LFM2.5-24B-A2B is the fastest of the compared MoEs, decoding 184 tokens/s on an M5 Max and 114 tokens/s on a Ryzen AI Max+ 395. That is up to 1.7x faster than the next-best model, while using the least memory.

GPU inference. LFM2.5-24B-A2B is the fastest model in its size class, reaching over 21K output tokens per second at high concurrency on a single B300.

Reach for LFM2.5-24B-A2B when you need agents that reason, call tools, and run reliably on your device.

Install the latest version of transformers (compatible with transformers>=5.0.0):

Serve LFM2.5-24B-A2B locally behind any OpenAI-compatible backend, then point your agent harness at it. For example, with Hermes Agent:

The port depends on your serving backend: llama.cpp and MLX use 8080, vLLM uses 8000, SGLang uses 30000, and LM Studio uses 1234. See the model card for OpenClaw and Pi configs, and our guide for the full setup. Check out our release blog for video examples.

Both LFM2.5-24B-A2B and LFM2.5-24B-A2B-Base are open-weight and available on Hugging Face today:

#9693. Phishing-Resistant Isn't Enough; Yubico Takes Aim at Identity-Verification Gap

News, news analysis, and commentary on the latest trends in cybersecurity technology.

The new YubiID service bridges identity verification with credential enrollment and recovery across existing identity platforms, closing a phishing-resistant authentication gap. Plus: post-quantum YubiKey beta.

Yubico wants to help employers verify a person's identity before enrolling login credentials — and again when the employee needs to regain access after losing a key or mobile device.

On Tuesday, the maker of YubiKey authentication devices unveiled YubiID, a subscription service entering limited early access that links identity verification with credential enrollment and account recovery. Announced at Yubico's inaugural YubiNation user conference in San Francisco this week, the service integrates with major identity providers, including Microsoft Entra, Okta, and Ping, and supports enrolling credentials on YubiKeys and mobile phones. This extends Yubico's reach to organizations that have decided against deploying hardware keys.

The launch addresses a growing recognition that protecting a login to be phishing-resistant is no longer enough. It does not establish that the right person received the credential or that someone requesting a replacement is the legitimate owner. Yubico field CTO Derek Hanson described that shift at the FIDO Alliance's Authenticate conference last month, saying the help desk "has moved from an operational control to an actual security control in most enterprises."

Related:Cyera's Oasis Security Buy Is All About AI Agent Control

Yubico is working with a group of unnamed "large organizations" as design partners and hopes to make YubiID generally available in the first half of 2027, CEO Jerrod Chong tells Dark Reading. The company has not revealed pricing.

According to Chong, the problem YubiID addresses used to be an afterthought: confirming that a key reaches the right person and that someone reporting it as lost is that person. The new service provides a baseline identity-verification capability, but customers can also use their own verification process or rely on other providers. Planned integrations with Clear, Nametag, and HYPR will allow organizations to combine providers whose coverage differs by region.

For most enterprises, this is a familiar scenario: Employees prove their identities to HR in one part of the office, then collect their login credentials from IT in another part. Connecting these steps reduces opportunities for impersonation because identity verification is required for both initial enrollment and enrollment of replacement credentials.

"Recovery is such a weak spot for credential management," Andrew Shikiar, executive director and CEO of the FIDO Alliance, tells Dark Reading.

Digital identity credentials provide enterprises with a way to reestablish a user's identity during recovery without relying on knowledge-based secrets, he says. Solving the recovery challenge involves more than just technology; it also requires policy, regulatory alignment, user behavior change, and business process design.

Related:USA Fencing Lunges Into the Hidden Identity Challenge in Amateur Sports

For organizations already investing in Okta, Ping, or Microsoft Entra, YubiID coordinates verification and enrollment; it does not replace those identity platforms. Yubico has built connectors to enroll credentials from those providers and also supports homegrown identity systems.

"We're not being an IDP," Chong says. "I think that there are more opportunities for collaboration than competition."

The practical benefit is tighter coordination. An organization can connect its chosen verification process to enrollment in the identity systems employees already use, rather than managing those steps as disconnected workflows. That becomes especially relevant for enterprises running multiple identity providers, where the employee's immediate need is simply to receive working credentials, regardless of which platform manages the account.

For a company onboarding 10,000 temporary workers ahead of the holiday season, YubiID can support both administrator-assisted, in-person enrollment and remote enrollment and verification. The benefit of giving the company multiple ways to connect identity checks to access setup, Chong says, is as much operational as security-related — fewer disconnected steps between verifying a worker and getting that person authenticated — though he did not provide figures on potential time savings or reductions in help-desk work. Interest is strongest among organizations with large, distributed, or seasonal workforces, including transportation, retail, healthcare, consulting, and global services companies.

Related:Flaws in Passkey Implementation Show Old Attacks Still Work

Yubico is entering a market where identity providers and verification specialists already offer overlapping onboarding and recovery capabilities. Microsoft Entra's verified account recovery became generally available in May, using identity verification to help users regain access and register authentication methods without relying on a conventional manual help-desk process. Nametag and HYPR — both planned YubiID integration partners — also sell workforce verification and recovery capabilities. Beyond Identity already connects Nametag's identity checks to passkey enrollment and recovery, while 1Kosmos combines identity verification with passwordless authentication.

YubiID's differentiator is connecting verification and enrollment across platforms, rather than tying the workflow to a single identity provider, Chong maintains. Yubico also brings its hardware business into those relationships: It makes the devices where many customers' authentication credentials reside. Chong connects that experience with the challenge of distributing keys, verifying recipients, and enrolling replacements across a global workforce.

Hardware is not required. Support for credentials on mobile devices could appeal to customers who find hardware key distribution too difficult. Those customers haven't necessarily rejected the keys' security benefits; rather, the logistics are "sometimes quite challenging," Chong says.

Federal agencies could also use employees' existing PIV credentials to establish their identities when enrolling FIDO credentials on YubiKeys or mobile authenticators, Chong says, while noting that those workflows are future potential capabilities and not fully available at launch.

Separately, Yubico announced a public beta program for a post-quantum-ready YubiKey. The beta YubiKey will support NIST-standardized post-quantum algorithms, though it did not specify which ones. Yubico has tested early implementations with Chrome and Firefox, with early keys sent to federal labs and hyperscalers. The company expects to submit the key for FIPS validation within about a year, depending on beta testing and customer feedback, although completion is not guaranteed.

Despite being "crypto-agile," Chong confirms that the beta devices cannot receive firmware upgrades, meaning organizations would later need to replace those keys if different algorithms are required.

"Doing firmware upgrades safely across the Web is not trivial," he says.

A June executive order directs agencies to transition high-value assets and high-impact systems to post-quantum cryptography for key establishment by the end of 2030 and digital signatures by the end of 2031. Organizations evaluating the beta keys will need to test both the new cryptography and the process for replacing and enrolling devices.

Yubico ultimately envisions providing verifiable proof that a person authorized a specific AI agent action, but Chong confirms that agent-authorization capabilities are not part of this launch. While the combination of Yubico's back-end services, applications, and hardware keys forms the foundation for additional use cases, for now the YubiID service focuses on verifying people, enrolling credentials, and handling recovery.

"In a simple way to look at it, we're offering an end-to-end solution rather than just a YubiKey solution," Chong says.

Jeffrey Schwartz is a New York–based freelance writer specializing in information security and enterprise IT. Focused on the constant pace of technological change, Jeff has covered the evolution of technologies, including professional broadcast, computing, networking, the Internet, mobile communications, modern cloud infrastructure and software development for over 30 years.

Jeff has contributed to Dark Reading since 2022 and has written for Channel Futures for over five years. Before launching his freelance career, he was an editor at 1105 Media, where he served as editor-in-chief of Redmond magazine and contributed to its sister publications, including Redmond Channel Partner, Application Development Trends, and Virtualization Review.

Previously, Jeff held editorial roles at CMP Media’s CommunicationsWeek, InternetWeek, and VARBusiness. #9691. Welcome FLUX.3 Image Klein in Diffusers

Black Forest Labs FLUX.3 Image Klein is here, and it runs in Diffusers from day one. One model does text-to-image and multi-reference image-to-image, and it adds something new, the layout control. You write bounding boxes into the prompt to say where each part of the image should go, or which parts of a reference image to move.

Both open checkpoints are in the FLUX.3 Image Klein collection:

You can head on to the Hugging Face space and generate some images right now!

Install the latest diffusers and transformers (for the Qwen3-VL text encoder):

Load the distilled checkpoint and generate an image:

FLUX.3 responds best to a full scene description with the subject, the setting, the light, the composition, and the style. The official prompting guide from Black Forest Labs has more tips. The distilled checkpoint generates a 1024 × 1024 image in 16 steps by default. Pass height, width, or num_inference_steps to change them.

Pass a reference image (or more) with the image argument. Write the prompt as a caption of the image you want, with the change included.

With several references, refer to them in the prompt as , , ... in the order they are passed to image:

Add a JSON list of regions after the caption. Each region has an id, a bbox, and a desc, and the caption mentions it as .

Boxes are written as [y_min, x_min, y_max, x_max], y first, on a 0–1000 scale. Because the scale is normalized, the same box works at any image size.

For edits, each region says where its content comes from (src_bbox in the reference) and where it goes (tgt_bbox in the output). A region with the same two boxes stays where it is.

This example moves the knitted knight up and to the left, and pins the backdrop, the cliff, the needle, the dragon, and the fire:

Everything above uses the distilled checkpoint. The base checkpoint runs 50 steps with classifier-free guidance, and it's the one to fine-tune (see LoRA finetuning).

Black Forest Labs also ships the transformer as a single file, in bf16 and in two quantized formats: fp8r (rowwise FP8) and nvfp4. Load any of them with from_single_file, then load the other components by name so the bf16 transformer isn't downloaded too.

For the unquantized single file, use https://huggingface.co/{model_id}/blob/main/model.safetensors and drop quantization_config.

FLUX.3 works for both text-to-image and image-to-image, which makes it a great base for custom LoRAs. diffusers ships DreamBooth LoRA training scripts for both tasks (you can also train with Ostris' AI Toolkit).

Here is a text-to-image example that learns a tarot-card style from the multimodalart/1920-raider-waite-tarot-public-domain dataset, triggered with trtcrd:

To reduce memory usage, add a few optimization flags:

--gradient_checkpointing recomputes activations in the backward pass (lower VRAM, slightly slower), --cache_latents pre-encodes the images and frees the VAE, and --use_8bit_adam keeps the optimizer states in 8-bit.

A couple of knobs are worth experimenting with. The grid below trains the same tarot style with different LoRA ranks and optimizers; the adapters are on the Hub at diffusers-modular/flux3-tarot-lora. More training features and configurations are documented in the DreamBooth FLUX.3 README.

For instruction-based editing, the image-to-image script (train_dreambooth_lora_flux3_klein_img2img.py) trains on (reference image, target image, instruction) triplets, where the reference is addressed in the prompt as .

See the DreamBooth FLUX.3 README for all options and the full image-to-image example.

In this section, we will talk about the memory consumption and the speed of generation of the models.

End-to-end timings for the distilled checkpoint (16 steps), averaged over three runs after a warmup:

Single NVIDIA H100 80GB, no offloading, default attention backend.

A reference image roughly doubles the time. Reference tokens join the same sequence as the text and the image being generated, so a 1024 × 1024 reference adds 4,096 tokens to every transformer call

Let's open the model up, one piece at a time. The model takes three kinds of tokens:

FLUX.3 is a latent-space flow model for image generation. This means that the denoiser takes latents as inputs and produces latents as outputs. We use a VAE to decode the latents back to pixels. FLUX.3 uses the same VAE architecture as Flux.2.

The FLUX.2 VAE compresses an image 8× in each direction into 32 channels, and then every 2 × 2 patch of that latent is packed into a single token with 128 channels.

So one token covers a 16 × 16 pixel patch, and a 1024 × 1024 image becomes a 64 × 64 grid of 4,096 tokens. The noisy image starts as random noise of exactly that shape. A reference image goes through the same VAE encoder and packing, and keeps its own size.

The text encoder is Qwen3-VL, a vision-language model. FLUX.3 doesn't just take its last layer. It reads the hidden states of eight of its 36 layers (layers 4, 8, …, 32) and stacks them, so each text token becomes a 8 × 2560 = 20,480-dimensional vector before a linear layer projects it to the transformer's width of 3072.

This gives the transformer features from several depths of the language model, not just its final layer. The prompt is padded to a multiple of 80 tokens, and the transformer attends to the padding too, which is why the pipeline takes one prompt per call.

The transformer processes the tokens in two stages:

The two stages differ in who can attend to whom.

In stage 1, each stream only attends to itself, so each kind of token gets refined on its own terms first. In stage 2, everything attends to everything, where the image learns from the text and from the references. For comparison, FLUX.2's double-stream blocks also give text and image separate weights, but let them attend to each other from the start. FLUX.3 keeps the streams fully apart first, then merges them.

At the end, the text and reference tokens are simply dropped. Only the image tokens go through the output layers, which predict how to move them one step toward a clean image.

Every block, in either stage, has the same shape. Attention and the MLP run in parallel on the same normalized input, and their sum is added back to the residual stream.

Each block starts with a LayerNorm that has no learned scale or shift of its own. The scale, shift, and gate come from a timestep embedding instead (this is called modulation). Inside the attention, the queries and keys are RMS-normalized and get rotary position embeddings (RoPE), which we look at below.

In a joint block, all tokens share the same weights, but text, image, and reference tokens each get their own scale, shift, and gate.

In FLUX.1 and FLUX.2, one timestep embedding modulates every token. In FLUX.3, the modulation depends on the kind of token.

The noisy image tokens are modulated by the current timestep t. The text and reference tokens are always modulated by timestep 0, which means "clean, nothing to denoise here". So even a reference that looks almost the same as the output is marked as given context, not as something to generate.

The distilled checkpoint is a flow map. It is also told the timestep each step jumps to. That second timestep gets its own embedding, which is added to every token's modulation, so each of its 16 steps can make a larger jump.

Attention on its own doesn't know where a token is (this phenomenon is called permutation equivariance). RoPE fixes that by rotating each query and key by an amount that depends on the token's position. FLUX.3 uses four position axes, (t, h, w, l) (timestep, height, width, length of sequence), and gives each one a quarter (32 dimensions) of every 128-dimensional attention head:

Text tokens line up along l, like words in a sentence. The image and the references are 2D grids in (h, w), separated from each other along l. Because a reference uses the same (h, w) coordinates as the output, "the same spot in the reference" has a precise meaning to the model, which is what the src_bbox / tgt_bbox editing relies on.

FLUX.3 is a flow-matching model. Generation starts from pure noise, and at each of the 50 steps the transformer predicts a velocity. This is the direction from noise toward a clean image. The scheduler takes one step along it.

At every step you can also read off the model's current guess of the final image. Decoding that guess at a few steps shows how the image takes shape:

The fox, its pose, and the light are already in place by step 10, while the noise level is still 0.97. The snow-laden branches and the texture of the fur only appear in the last few steps. FLUX.3's scheduler uses a large time shift (6.93), which keeps the noise level high for most of the run: 44 of the 50 steps happen above σ = 0.5. We built this figure by adding one small block to the pipeline, which brings us to Modular Diffusers.

If you are new to flow matching, we have a beginner friendly tutorial and a video for you to understand how it works.

FLUX.3 ships as a Modular Diffusers pipeline.

You can list the workflows and print the exact blocks of each one, without loading any weights.

get_workflow() resolves the auto branches and gives you the plain sequence of steps that will run. print(blocks.get_workflow("image_conditioned").doc) prints the components, inputs, defaults, and outputs of that workflow.

Pop the text encoder out, encode the prompt once, free it, and generate from the cached embeddings.

The denoising figure above came from one extra block that records the model's guess of the clean image at every step:

Built something with FLUX.3? Share your LoRAs and pipelines on the Hub. We'd love to see them! 😎

InfoQ Homepage Presentations Panel: Who Builds the Frontend Now? (And What Breaks When They Do)

The panelists explain how AI tools and vibe coding reshape frontend and mobile engineering. They share insights on evolving junior developer roles, managing AI-generated code review fatigue, designing systems for autonomous agents, enforcing architectural guardrails, and navigating economic shifts in open-source software sustainability.

Luca Mezzalira is an independent software architect, consultant, and educator. James Hall is Founder and Director @Parallax and Author of jsPDF. Danielle An is a Principal Engineer at Meta Horizon. Ivan Zarea is Director of Platform Engineering at Netlify. Panel moderated by Ian Thomas, Software Engineer @Meta.

Software is changing the world. QCon London empowers software development by facilitating the spread of knowledge and innovation in the developer community. A practitioner-driven conference, QCon is designed for technical team leads, architects, engineering directors, and project managers who influence innovation in their teams.

Presented by: David Iparraguirre - Senior Product Marketing Manager at Datadog, and Jessica Yang - Product Manager at Datadog

Thomas: We're going to have a bunch of themes that we're going to explore together around the topic of the day, emerging trends in the frontend and mobile.

I just wanted to frame a little bit the landscape of what we're talking about here today, where we have this imbalance between adoption and trust, which is quite drastic. A significant drop in entry-level roles, framing the career growth aspect and thinking about what does it mean to be an engineer joining the ladder or being at the more senior end of the ladder these days. Then, what does it mean for us all if people can go and spend $1,000 in a week and rebuild one of the most mature frameworks in the frontend space with apparently very little effort? The three areas we're going to look at, the changing job, building for agents, and quality and trust.

Danielle An: I'm Danielle. I'm a principal engineer at Meta. My job is about essentially evolving the social gaming platform that we have into the AI era. A lot of mobile development, a lot of UI, UX, scaling into the hundreds of millions of people that use our ecosystem.

James Hall: I'm James. I run a company called Parallax. We help organizations build teams to build tech. I wrote some popular open-source Node stuff in the past, like jsPDF and things like that. We just help people build tech quite quickly.

Luca Mezzalira: My name is Luca. I'm a serverless specialist solution architect in AWS. Why I'm here? Because in the last 10 years, I mastered the idea of distributed systems on frontend. Wrote a book about micro-frontends. Currently, the architecture is embraced by the largest companies in the world. Think about Formula 1, PayPal, all the others. They're all drawing from the experience that I describe inside the book and very often they refer to. That's why I'm here.

Ivan Zarea: I'm Ivan. I am a director of platform at Netlify. My responsibility is hosting everything, including some of your personal projects. I'm on call for some of them. We're also working with a bunch of framework authors, open-source communities, and making sure that things are evolving in the web framework space.

Thomas: A year ago, vibe coding was a tweet. Now Y Combinator are saying that their last batch shipped 95% AI-generated codebases. With that in mind and the changing landscape of entry-level frontend roles, I'm really curious how you're seeing these changes impact the hiring and the training and the landscape for you internally in your companies and how you're thinking about what frontend engineers and developers really need in this day and age.

James Hall: I think we need both ends. We need super senior, experienced people who've got all the battle scars. Then you also need the naive junior engineers who have only known of a world where ChatGPT exists. Because they try things that you would never think to do. They approach stuff in a very different way. They don't have those battle scars. It's like blending the two levels of experience, I think, is really important. I know a lot of people said that the junior roles are going to go away. I'm not seeing that at all. I'm seeing very much a need for it, actually.

Thomas: Have you changed anything around your hiring profiles that you're looking for?

James Hall: Yes. We actually allow people to use AI in their interview process, which is a blessing and a curse. You can sometimes see people really struggle with that, because they're trying to talk to and understand this huge stream of output from an LLM. It can actually be quite off-putting for some people to try and talk through that. Some senior engineers you see quite struggle with it. We've had to be quite pointed about how we test people and do a little bit more whiteboarding, a bit more conversation, like you used to, I suppose. Less of the like, can you code this thing in an editor?

Thomas: How are things looking from your perspective as a senior principal solutions architect?

Luca Mezzalira: I can tell you that in Amazon, in general, we have a lot of mid-level senior engineers on the frontend side. I speak with a lot of them. Because very often, when they are building their solution, they are looking into implementing micro-frontends. Therefore, I have the possibility to work with them very closely, even for migrations towards that topic. I think that, at least for us, is not going away at all. Even the CEO of AWS said very clearly, we are going to hire. The CEOs on the architecture side in my division, we are still hiring a lot of people coming straight from university. We are training them. The thing that I think in Amazon works always pretty well is the fact that we have mechanisms for mentorship and for helping others that maybe don't have the battle scars, James was saying. That I agree, it's not an easy thing to find. Having a mechanism, being intentional, basically, helps a ton.

Thomas: With the widening range of people building frontends, and this is going to speak directly to what Ivan was sharing earlier, how are you thinking about access to non-technical roles within your organizations, and how that's being coached and developed?

Danielle An: When you say non-technical, are you talking about non-engineers?

Thomas: We're thinking about anybody that might be interested in building a tool. It could be any department. We've had examples in Ivan's talk from people in HR, the CFO. We've got product managers. The list is almost endless as who's got access now and capability.

Also, vibe coding nowadays, we're joking in the team, we'll just take for granted it's going to work on the frontend for the most part, especially if you're prototyping. If you're trying to get ideas across, you're not thinking about something scaling into the billions where there's lots of account issues and lots of stuff that needs to be worked out. If you want to bring ideas, prototype your app, something you're imagining, something you are stuck in traffic and you think this will really help with that, and you go home and you vibe that, there's just a ton of opportunity for everybody. People that have the right ideas, even if you're not a coder, you can pretty much use Claude to get 80% there. Maybe you need a little bit of help, you got some coworkers to help out with that. I just think there's a ton of excitement there.

Ivan Zarea: We also see this trend. For example, our UX team vibe coded a NPS survey that actually integrates within our app very well and is not like a third party that is integrated through an iframe or something like that. There's lots of opportunity there for people who are domain experts to actually leverage their domain expertise. One challenge that I see with that, and for us as a community of engineers or as frontenders is what that done means, because to someone who is not an engineer or doesn't have that engineering expertise, to them it works on my machine, or it works in my Claude is kind of done. Then you either get the engineering team overwhelmed with a bunch of pull requests to review and like, who do you give the comments to? Is the model going to fix them or is the UX designer going to fix them?

Additionally, it creates debt, it creates a mess that we will need to figure out how to maintain. It forces us to get our stuff together and figure out how do we want our frontends to evolve given that there's a lot more people contributing to them who are not necessarily the same level of skill. Additionally, that's not only applicable to frontend engineers. It is very easy for backenders to be like, how hard can React be. I can just vibe code this thing and then you end up with a couple of Redux actions and here you go, what up? As anyone who has maintained a large codebase knows that there's a lot of debt that comes with that. There's a lot of architectural challenges that comes with that. There's a lot of deep expertise in the frontend space that is not immediately visible and that is hidden behind like, this is the frontend that you build. We do see this challenge as well, not only coming from non-technical people, but also just non-frontend people who do not have that deep expertise in the frontend space.

James Hall: I think one challenge is that it sets people's expectations of the speed that you can move in a large enterprise incorrectly as well, because enterprises are set up to do careful checks, do testing, SOC compliance, ISO, all that stuff that you need to keep your organization together. When someone from a non-technical role can vibe code an entire five-step onboarding wizard in an afternoon, they think, surely, we can make the rest of the process happen in a couple of days to get this live, and it's just not the case. This is where we're butting up against legal, compliance, testing, QA, all that stuff. It's like, if you optimize one bit, how do you optimize all the rest of it? That's where we're going to see a real challenge.

Luca Mezzalira: I think very often we try to think about, ok, so vibe coding, therefore I can create software. Coding is a chunk of the software. In the software development life cycle, there is a tiny portion that is called, ok, we need to write some code. There is the 80% or more of the software development life cycle that is not coding, and therefore we need to be aware of that. I think, probably I'm a boring architect, but we need guardrails that prevents us to arrive to a point where we really think that a PM can write code that is perfectly aligned with all the best practices in the company that can be integrated in no time into a system. We need to be careful on that. Every context has some rules, every context has some difficulties and challenges. Working in a regulated environment that requires a certain level of resilience, capabilities, throughput, latency, is not the same as creating a website for an expo or a conference.

It's completely different. Very often what I'm noticing with customer backend and frontend doesn't really matter, to be honest, is that they don't ask the right questions. Currently, I think the industry is hidden behind the idea of, we can vibe code whatever. Yes, but this whatever, it might not be inside your context. For instance, I really like talking with Malte Ubl, the CTO of Vercel, their process where they say, ok, we created V0 for design and developers. In reality, we created for PMs, because their PMs currently, they are thinking about a new idea or a new feature. They create a mock with V0 and then they pass the ball to the developers, but they create strong guardrails on that. You have an idea, you can show how it would look like, how it should feel so you can realize what works, what doesn't, and that's the first feedback loop that we have.

Then we have the second one that is moving into production, and production is not straight away what, let's say, is just some code. Production is way more because there are a lot of checks. Probably you can tell quite a lot of stories operating Netlify at a scale that is incredibly difficult. It's not a walk in the park.

Thomas: I saw an interview with Peter Steinberger, the OpenClaw creator, who said that one of the things that his tooling has provided is the access for people to contribute, and the overwhelming nature of PRs that he gets on his project is overwhelming. The thing he does is he doesn't take them verbatim, he takes them as prompts and intent, and then translates that into what his vision of the product should be. Do you think this is potentially a way of working that we should be doubling down on or is this something that we're seeing as a nascent practice so that PMs and designers and folks can have their input but it's taken as a guide rather than the final artifact?

Danielle An: I feel really passionate about this one, because again, I think gaming is just about if it connects with people. Usually, so much gaming content is the first 20 seconds, are you interested or not? If you're not, you have moved on. I think a lot of what you're talking about is how do we bring prototypes into production, and this makes the product actually sticky. I think right now, probably at every company, what we see is everybody's like, look at the shiny thing I did. Day and night, 24/7 with Claws and stuff like that. I think what's tricky is that everybody can build to a certain depth. Like, this is cool, but it's only cool once, it's only cool for the first minute. Then going beyond that, which makes it something that lots of people really want in the longer term or lots of people would want even just for days, I don't think that problem is solved because we can vibe code.

I think it just brings a lot of creativity to the surface where anybody can be like, look at my puppy, and I put something on my puppy, isn't that funny? Like, that's great. Beyond that, the next level of creativity that people really want and we all crave, I think still, it needs to be cultivated. Vibe coding just removes a barrier, but it doesn't suddenly make everybody have this genius idea that connects with everybody else. I think it's a bit of like a bubble, a little bit of a hype.

Thomas: How many people are working in consultancy versus in an in-house team building a product? Given what you said before about expectations have been reset to be super-fast, what does that mean for the pricing model for a consultancy?

James Hall: I haven't quite figured that out yet. We still price based on FTEs. I think what it does do is it makes some projects that were seemingly unviable now viable. They might have priced it up, this is going to cost us £2 million. Actually, we could probably do it for $200,000. Why don't we quickly try and do that, test and learn, get an external outfit to do that. I'm trying not to be squeezed on price, but it is difficult.

Thomas: Let's move on to the second topic I wanted to focus on. Stefan's talk was going deep into some of the things behind computer usage of our things that we build. Keen to explore what happens when we realistically now serve two very different sorts of user. You've got the humans, the people here, and the people that don't have feelings, emotions and cognition, obviously the rest of it, with the agents that are using it. In particular, one thing I think would be interesting to explore is, what does trust mean in this world? Because, for example, if we were to look at a product and the way we designed it, we aim for a polish and a finesse and a design aesthetic that shows quality. What does that mean when a computer is interpreting it? They don't really have a concept of quality like that. I'm really curious how we need to start thinking as a cohort of people working on these clients and these mobile apps and websites. What does it mean to serve these two different types of user?

James Hall: I think what makes it good for a user makes it good for an AI. I think you're seeing this wave now of MCPs blasted open the floodgates, people are opening APIs a bit wider than they would have, people are connecting more data sources than ever. Actually, the CLI interface is super handy, because I don't know if you would even try to attempt to write out an MCP JSON blob by hand, you probably wouldn't. You would write Bash and you would pipe stuff and chain stuff. Actually, is the interface CLI, even if it is a virtual CLI? NVIDIA launched its sandbox CLI this week. Vercel have just Bash, which is a TypeScript implementation of Bash. Yes, can we create these super nice to use for humans SDKs that are super nice for AI as well? I think we can. You've seen Playwright MCP is now Playwright CLI, it's just come out. Loads nicer to use by hand. It goes back to all the good stuff that we used to do, like ReadMe driven development, like just keep it super simple, nice and easy to type, and that makes it good for AI as well.

Ivan Zarea: I'm going to slightly disagree here. I do foresee some recalibration happening in the industry where we do realize that there are certain tasks that agents are inherently better at than humans, because of the amount of processing they can do in the time. An example of that is, so I come from a platform background. I look at charts a lot to see if things are down or not. It's very difficult to teach agents to look at charts and understand them, but that is how my brain works. I would rather teach agents to look at time series data, and they can do that very well. They can look at a lot of time series data very quickly. This means that we're trying to design internal tooling to, instead of exposing human readable or human adjusted pre-aggregated signals, that actually there's a decision happening in the background of, is this signal going to be valuable for a human in order not to overwhelm the human?

We're able to expose like almost raw data. That is just one example of how I see kind of like, there's an interface that we thought would be better for humans, and actually for agents that there's a better interface. Same thing with some of the CLIs where if a CLI is interactive, it provides engagement for a human, but actually a simple long command is better for an agent. I do think that there's going to be some recalibration happening in exactly what you said about how do we define quality? Because this new cohort of users perceives quality in a different way. That doesn't mean we have to stop caring, but it just means caring for a slightly different audience.

Thomas: Trust signals are going to be massive. I'm curious about Danielle's view on this, because with a little bit of inside knowledge here, Horizon Worlds as a product over the years has evolved to have this very use case. UGC platform, people can come on, they can build worlds, they can build games, they can write the scripting. Then increasingly it's becoming AI first where people can prompt to do that. The AI needs to have access to all the capabilities that a human had. Is there anything that we learn in that journey that would be useful to help more broadly across the frontend and mobile landscape? Are there any key points that we hit where we decided something and then found actually, no, different ways is a better way?

Danielle An: I slightly disagree with you earlier, because I think that it is true, a lot of information agents can just see in raw format, even just in .md files is different. I don't read .md files as well. They do think differently. In reality, in particular, you're talking about UGC, when something goes wrong, which only happens in runtime, the agent is not sufficient to solve those all by itself. You do bring a human and the human has to work with the agent at the same time, if something is not working. I think if we design things to be either more agent things in binary chunks or whatever else, but the human comes in and doesn't think that at all. You're creating this barrier between the human and the agent collaborating when something goes horribly wrong. I think for UGC, things always go horribly wrong. Like the skirt is not tucked in and only under certain lighting, you would see a problem that looks like it's very inappropriate.

A lot of those things, I think, require you to think like, what did the agent need to understand that a human needs to debug? What also it can do that I don't care about at all, like data is not compressed or whatever, don't tell me that, just fix that. It was more something that is very visual, very runtime, very dynamic. Every run is unique. When that happens, I think the agent has to understand what a human needs, what a human is going to debug with, and how is a human going to look at this information, and help the human understand that. I think that's really important in our work.

Thomas: Given some of the things that have happened in Amazon recently where there has been agent accelerated SEVs, is there anything that we're learning about why agents can help us to make bad choices that we can put guardrails in, thinking more holistically in the way that we're building our guardrails and systems?

Luca Mezzalira: I don't have the full visibility on all the things that we are doing inside the engineering side, because obviously, as you can imagine, Amazon is a company with 1.8 million people. As you can imagine, it's difficult to have visibility on everything. That said, I think currently we are using heavily in general in our processes, agents. We are betting on AI heavily. We also developed Kiro as a fork of Visual Studio Code and CLI. We started to see, especially internally, a lot of tools bubbling around, built by engineers or by architects for helping us to increase the understanding of our business. In the latest few months, I've seen more tools than ever that started to bubble up in our npm repository of AI tools. The thing is, obviously, in order to operate properly, you need to have all your house in order. I have a few friends that were working in Meta and they explained to me how everything is automated, everything is well-suited.

I think Amazon grows organically. There are certain areas that work better than others. That's normal. Therefore, I think AI can augment or potentially replace certain activities better in this area that everything is well designed and oiled properly. While in other areas, it might struggle a bit because it will rely on patterns that are already implemented, learn from those patterns, and might not be the best patterns that you can find. For that, you cannot expect that you have the perfect outcome as you think. You need to first fix the issue, retrain, restart, and move on. This is good learnings for everyone, because the reality is not that AI will be, sprinkle magic everywhere and everything will be super amazing, unicorn everywhere. It will be an augmentation and it will help us to achieve more in a short amount of time. It can replace certain parts of our job. We need also to think that, again, if we provide wrong input, we are going to have a wrong output, inevitably. They cannot guess what we have in our head or what is intrinsically expressed inside the trenches.

Thomas: That neatly moves us on to the next block, which is, who's responsible? If we're putting these things out there, who ultimately is the person on the hook for all this code that's suddenly exploding into production?

Luca Mezzalira: Claude. We put Claude on call. Whatever is called Claude, it will be responsible. I strongly believe that we don't have to forget everything that we have done in the last 40 years in engineering. Especially in my experience in distributed systems, one of the key areas is that ownership is well defined. If you don't have clear ownership, then you don't expect that the system will work nicely. There are certain situations, like when I see large organizations implementing InnerSourcing that is basically open-source practices, but applying inside private repositories or projects where even there you have a team that is leading the project that accepts and revisits certain requests or discussions, like you were mentioning OpenClaw, for instance. I think those are not that are fading away. Now, the thing that I personally think about that is quite hilarious to a certain extent, that I think we will achieve more with the same amount of people or potentially with slightly less people, we achieve equal throughput of the past.

It seems like a classic circle in tech, because back in the days, when in frontend there was Flash, the same things that you could do in JavaScript with a team, we were doing with 1, 2 people max. With some performances that sometimes could result in a better thing, especially towards the end when you have access to GPU acceleration. We're talking about probably 15 years ago, if not more. That was quite fun for me seeing the after-Flash era where currently for doing something medium complex, you need like one or two teams for running that. That was quite hilarious. That's the thing that I draw from my experience.

James Hall: Who owns the code that they commit? It's got to be the engineer that commits it, you'd think. That causes a problem with AI fatigue, where you feel like you want to move really quickly, and you're opening PRs, getting colleagues to review, but you're having to review lots of other people's PRs as well. I think, I can't speak for everyone, but by the afternoon, you're full up now, that's enough reviews, you don't want to look at any more code. In a lot of organizations we've been working with, keeping the PR size really small has been extremely important. In fact, for some high-risk repos, 200 lines is the hard max, and that can be a little bit painful, but, for the right reasons, it's to make sure that everybody understands what's going on in the codebase. You've got someone else rubber stamping it. We use policy-bot, which is a GitHub project, quite widely, and we have team review and then risk review. It's tricky. The risk levels are going to be very different. If it's like a conference website, you might be able to just vibe the whole thing. It's probably ok, except for the registration form, maybe don't do that.

Danielle An: What I observe a lot nowadays is that engineers are not actually reading the code at all. When they check in, the other engineer also didn't want to read it, so they just all assume if it has passed, I just move on. Of course, like you said, that's ok for maybe QCon Conference, but that's not quite ok for a lot of things, like Meta, for example, does. I'm curious how you guys are enforcing that. It just seems impossible to enforce. I just see engineers fly by diffs like 20 a day, like nobody read this. It's like thousands of lines. How are you dealing with that?

Ivan Zarea: More specifically in our organization, there's a couple of things. On one hand, we also have helper bots that help review things. Also, we're investing in cross-service knowledge context that allows for bots to review things in a way that is context aware of how it affects other things. It's like a review with larger context, more like an architectural review. Finally, we're doubling down on in-person whiteboarding. We are a distributed company, so that makes it very difficult for us to meet. We do see that right now the speed of shipping has increased. That means that we need to be even more focused about drawing boxes and arrows and more disciplined about that. That is where the review and the brainstorming and the magic happens. Then the code implementation is a byproduct of that.

James Hall: I'd agree with that. Something else that we found quite useful is getting different models to do the reviewing than the models used to write them. Gemini for review, let's say, and Claude to write it. Gemini, we would write a file for it, which is based on the last hundred or last thousand PRs that have been merged. You can get Claude to just go and grab all the comments and all the nits, each team have got their own style, and try and encode that as well as possible into the review guidelines. Then when someone's reviewing it, it looks and feels like that project. It doesn't look like it was written by Claude.

James Hall: Only for review time. Maybe it doesn't.

Ivan Zarea: If you've ever had a conversation between a Gemini and a Libra, then you would understand that they do not work well together.

Thomas: It's interesting, I guess to a point you made earlier, Luca, about that we shouldn't forget about the things that have happened in the past. I think the DORA reports from the last couple of years just reinforced that. We see now that, yes, there's greater throughput, but the size of the batch is bigger. We know from many years of research that that leads to poorer engineering outcomes. It comes back to that tension again between the engineers may have had this training and this experience. There may be a new batch of engineers that don't get that experience, which is partly what this Anthropic report around debugging skills reducing in more junior engineers because they're more AI friendly. Also, the whole cohort that we've talked about before about people who are not engineers at all don't identify as that. Luca Mezzalira: Personally, I have a mental model usually applied with every enterprise customer that I follow. Again, I'm working mainly with enterprises, so take with a pinch of salt. If you're working at a startup, the practice could be different. In my case, usually is a matter of understanding the team system and then understanding the socio-technical system. Plus dividing the system in subdomains and categorize them. In domain-driven design, there is this idea of core, generic, and supporting domain that you can assign characteristics to. At my previous company, when I was working in DAZN, that is a live sports streaming platform, we categorize the whole system in these subdomains and we assign capabilities. We assign a certain seniority of developers based on the domain that they were working on. These things help us also to define these practices. Because if I'm thinking in a generic domain or in a supporting domain, very often you buy more than building because are less important.

If you think about payment for Netflix, nowadays they build their own payment gateway, but in the past they didn't. They were just aggregating PayPal, Stripe, and all the others. This is integration. The type of engineering practices they apply and the way you use AI could be heavy. While if you are building on the heuristics of the video player, that basically for a company like Netflix is the most important thing, because it's the reason why it exists, there you need to be careful because you cannot have heuristics that are changed randomly inside the video player because it could affect the experience for the user. As you can see now, if you start to segment your software into subdomains and apply different characteristics and approaches, then you start to have high throughput in certain areas and maybe you are more careful in others. If you replay exactly the same example in banks, usually that's what happens. Ivan Zarea: We do have a bunch of things here breaking in practice due to AI-generated code, and I'm curious, you mentioned that AI can cross-review itself or a different agent can review itself. James Hall: AI is quite dramatically bad for security because the hackers are using AI and also people on the other side are using AI to generate quick prototypes using like Supabase. When AI gets stuck, the first thing it does is switch off the security problem. Like row-level security on Supabase or something, like it'll just flip that off immediately. That's where hackers come in and they're using AI to quickly blast lots of endpoints because people that are new to building apps, they don't realize that let's encrypt certificates, broadcast as a transparency log, and as soon as you publish them into the internet with an SSL certificate, hackers are at it already. Bots are trying to poke it, prod it, all the rest of it. LLMs can very quickly see if they can go sideways and do other nasty things across your infrastructure. Yes, it's like gasoline on the fire, isn't it? It's both ends. I don't know if this is a good fix. Claude reckon they've got a new security tool coming out. I don't know if that'll be any good.

Luca Mezzalira: We don't have to forget what we have done so far. It seems, apart from the hype, there's this idea where LLMs are in the center of our life now. I think we need to treat them as a tool more often than not at the moment. If I think of any other revolution that happened in software, we always treated the new things as a tool. It was part of an architecture. It was part of a software development life cycle. It wasn't the center of everything. That means we built in the past fantastic tools that enables through different techniques to test the software end-to-end on security side. Now, are they perfect? Maybe not. Is AI perfect? No. We know upfront. If we are capable to combine the two things and not creating a mutual exclusive decision, like we want to use only AI for doing everything, I think we will land in a very nice place, because now one tool that is deterministic majority of the time because they do static analysis, abstract syntax tree, they do a bunch of checks around the system, you will be able to have the best of both worlds.

I personally believe that in certain areas, despite currently if they are good or not, there is still the need of a deterministic output, that we like it or not. Even on UI, for instance, I strongly believe that there are areas that can be probabilistic, other areas that shouldn't be probabilistic. Some other things, in my opinion, is that we need to look holistically again on the software development life cycle and identify what we accept that could be a drift, that is not the ideal outcome that we expect. Others instead that we say, hang on, we want to use SonarQube, or we want to make sure that static analysis and cyclomatic complexity reaches a certain point if we still care about code, because that's another good question that was raised during this conference in several ways. Danielle An: Actually, one of the main things we have is, again, we have artists, we have game designers here, is that in the past, I think artists and game designers were blocked by what an engineer can write in code such that people can experience that thing, whatever the game is. When you can do that, it's very interesting. Should we get money when we publish onto some social platform and a million people played it? The cost probably was clawed in $200 per person, 5 people, like $1,000. Whereas in the past, even just to ship something like that, you need so many cycles of engineering time, it easily would be 10 times more expensive or even more than that.

I think the bigger question here, I don't know if anybody actually has answers, is how the tokens between the creator of the content and the player of the content and the platform that hosts that content is going to scale up in a way where they all want to do it? If creators don't want to do it because they're not making money, it's going to burn the whole economy. If the platform is like, you guys are all having fun, but I'm not making money, so it's also not going to work. I think that dynamic just entirely shifts from there's a budget as if I'm making a movie and it could be $200 million that I already got for my game. It takes 18 months. It can make or break my studio. To like, ok, so we have cool ideas and it may only take $500 to prompt that. Then, how do I distribute that? How do I get this content to be ranked very high and discovered? How do I get to the right audience? I think it's going to be very disruptive, but in a very exciting way. I don't think there's any answers yet.

Thomas: What do we think about the Tailwind model?

James Hall: You may not know, but our head of frontend left us to be employee number one at Tailwind back in the day. Brad worked on the Tailwind VS Code extension while he was working at Parallax, and went over to there to build out their premium offering. I think it's super interesting. I was never able to monetize any of my open-source stuff, even though it's super popular, because I couldn't figure out a way to hamper it to then upsell something else. I think it was always on tenuous ground. You relied on people going to the website, going, I like this pack of this is how you use Tailwind for these problems, and I'm going to drop $59 or whatever, it's inconsequential for a big company. You get enough of those, and then you can build a team. That's what the Tailwind guys were doing, and gals.

I think they did very well, but I think they were in a quite precarious situation. I do think open source, that classic XKCD diagram, isn't it? It's like there's some thankless maintainer just maintaining one lib that holds up the whole thing. I don't know if I've got a good solution. I don't think it's going to get any better. It's certainly getting a lot worse. I'm seeing lots of contributions to open-source projects that are literally just vibe coded by OpenClaw or whatever, and a lot of pull requests on jsPDF and others that are just automatically closed, because it's just like, this is just rubbish. This GitHub open by default, anyone can open a PR thing, they're going to have to switch that at some point, because it's too much. Open-source maintainers have been ignored and underappreciated for a long time, and I think this has just accelerated that.

Participant 1: Do you think we will reach a point where the sheer quantity of code that's been generated and just repeatedly over and over again, that the core understanding is just lost? In terms of like nitpicky kind of, this problem P is here, that that is just completely absent. We have to lean on, ok, I need a general thing to understand this. Like, we all know that one engineer that you give them a bug and they're like, "Yes, I know what file that's in. It's here. I'm going to change that, done." Do you think that that is going to disappear?

James Hall: I think you do find when you're using AI, you almost feel like you're losing your abilities a little bit. I don't know if anyone else feels like that. I do think that muscle memory and being able to remember functions and how things stitch together does go away a bit. It goes to your point earlier about whiteboarding and having a clear picture. I think you just need to take yourself away from a computer, draw some boxes and have a walk, get some fresh air. I think hopefully it doesn't go away, but I could probably see a world where it does.

Thomas: Maybe I can offer a counter point to that slightly. I've had a very similar feeling about owning codebases and knowing about code and being the expert on it for a long time. Then I went to Meta where there is so much more code than I could ever imagine. I did try for a brief moment to understand it all, but it's not going to ever happen. I think people have to adopt a more large codebase mindset where you're never going to be the expert on everything, but you have to be the expert on finding the information. It's about adapting your techniques to identify and triage and then hone in on something, which again, going back a step is quite worrying to see the debugging trends going backwards. At some point you reach a point where you can't understand everything anyway, whether you've got AI or not. I think those techniques are really critical skills to develop in the future.

Ivan Zarea: I think this part of the craft is going to die out eventually. I see this trend actually somewhere in a different place. I see this trend in like support organizations, oftentimes where I've talked to customers and I see like, how did their support organizations operate? What is interesting is that, a lot of the time, support organizations were optimizing for solving numbers of tickets. With an increased influx of tickets, you cannot humanly sift through them. Then the natural answer is, ok, hire more support people. That actually decreases the quality of your support because then you have like endbrain sifting through this. Then it's a challenge to transition to a higher level where you're not looking at an individual ticket or an individual request and are using data to sift through trends and understand what's happening. I think that this is what we're expecting in our industry as well, where that part of the craft is going to slowly die out in certain areas like FFmpeg, like that XKCD comic that you mentioned. There are certain areas in which that is still going to continue. As a general rule for most of us, it's probably going to die out.
