#9641. Self-host live updates for Capacitor with Codemagic Patch

Codemagic Patch ships live updates of HTML, CSS, and JavaScript to Capacitor, Ionic, and Cordova-on-Capacitor apps, without a new store binary.

Say a checkout button stops working on some Android 15 devices, and the fix turns out to be four lines of TypeScript. In a Capacitor app, those four lines live in the web layer, inside a WebView, nowhere near native code. Without over-the-air (OTA) updates, they still have to go the long way round: new binary, store submission, review, and then a slow trickle of users who eventually update. Some never do.

That’s the problem OTA updates solve. While we originally developed it for React Native apps, Codemagic Patch now also supports Capacitor apps with our self-hosted tool.

Patch v0.6.0 ships with two new packages: @codemagic/capacitor-patch, the SDK that goes into your app, and @codemagic/capacitor-patch-cli, a command line made for publishing and managing Capacitor releases. They use the same server, dashboard, and delivery protocol as our React Native SDK.

Below, we’ll go through what you get with Patch, why Capacitor turned out to be the simplest framework we’ve ever built OTA support for, how you can self-host Patch, and where to find the docs to get your first release out.

Ionic has announced that all Appflow features and services will be sunset on December 31, 2027, a little over a year from now. They’ll keep Appflow up to date with its dependencies until then. After that, Ionic warns that apps still depending on Appflow may hit failed builds and failed live updates, and users may end up looking at a blank white screen.

A year can feel like plenty of time. It isn’t, once you account for how an OTA migration works. Your new SDK has to ship inside a native binary. That binary has to pass review and then actually get installed by enough of your users, because every device still on the old SDK will keep asking the old service for updates. In practice, the migration build should be out months before the deadline.

We’ve been building, signing, and publishing Capacitor apps on Codemagic for years, and Ionic’s own continuity page lists us as an alternative for Appflow native builds. Capacitor teams could also already get OTA updates from our CodePush service through the community cap-codepush plugin. Patch replaces that arrangement with a first-party SDK that we design, test, and support ourselves. For a Capacitor team, that means native builds and live updates from one vendor.

A server you can run yourself, an SDK in the app, a CLI to publish the web build you already produce, and a dashboard for what happened after that.

The Codemagic Patch dashboard with example data

OTA for React Native is a fairly involved piece of engineering. The tooling has to deal with a bundler (Metro or Expo), Hermes bytecode, and the New Architecture, and it has to hook into both how the bundle is built and how the runtime loads it.

Capacitor has none of that. A Capacitor app is a native shell that points a WebView at a folder of web assets, and @capacitor/core already has the APIs to change which folder that is (setServerBasePath, getServerBasePath, and persistServerBasePath). An OTA update comes down to downloading a new folder, verifying it, and pointing Capacitor at it on the next launch. There’s no bundler to integrate with and no bytecode format to match.

You see the same thing in the CLI. cmpatch-capacitor doesn’t run your build and doesn’t care whether you’ve run npx cap sync. You build the way you already do (ionic build, ng build, vite build), and whatever lands in your webDir is the release. It doesn’t matter whether that’s Angular, React, Vue, or Svelte.

Fewer moving parts means fewer ways for an update to break your app, and for an update mechanism that’s the property that counts most.

There’s one rule every team should understand before shipping their first Capacitor OTA release, because it’s much cheaper to learn it now than in production.

Your web bundle calls into native code: Capacitor plugins, your own native classes, native configuration. A bundle built for one native build can break on another. If your new web code calls Camera.getPhoto() and the installed binary shipped before you added @capacitor/camera, it will fail.

The Capacitor CLI doesn’t try to detect this by fingerprinting your native project. Every release instead targets one exact native app version (CFBundleShortVersionString on iOS, versionName on Android) and is only delivered to that version. Ranges and wildcards aren’t accepted. In day-to-day terms:

If your team already versions carefully, you’ll hardly notice this. If it doesn’t, OTA will push you into the habit, and you’ll be better off for it. The binary version filter added to the Patch dashboard’s deployment and Metrics pages in this release makes it easy to see how each version is doing.

Put together, every change goes down one of two paths:

Build your web assets, publish them with cmpatch-capacitor release create against the current binary version, test on Staging, then promote to Production with a staged rollout.

Bump the native version, then build, sign, and publish through Codemagic. Once the new binary is through review and in users’ hands, future OTA releases target the new version.

OTA is easy to oversell, so it’s worth being specific.

The obvious win is speed. A web-layer fix stops taking days of review and update lag and starts reaching users within minutes of publishing, as soon as their devices check in. For a consumer app, that can be the difference between a wave of one-star reviews and nobody noticing. For a B2B or internal app, it’s the difference between an escalation and a ticket closed the same afternoon.

You also end up supporting fewer versions. With store-only updates, every version a user hasn’t bothered to update is still out there, still generating bug reports. With OTA, devices on the same binary converge on the same web bundle, so “can’t reproduce” happens a lot less.

And your two release cycles can run at their own pace. The native release train can stay as deliberate as your compliance process requires, monthly or quarterly, while the web layer ships whenever your team is ready. Staging, staged rollouts, and promotion give you a controlled route from merge to full rollout.

What OTA can’t do is ship native code, and the app stores are explicit about where that line is.

Apple’s Developer Program License Agreement, section 3.3.1(B) forbids apps from downloading executable code but allows interpreted code, which is what the JavaScript in a Capacitor WebView is. There are conditions. The downloaded code can’t change the app’s primary purpose by adding features that don’t match how the app was described and advertised. It can’t get around signing, sandboxing, or other OS security features. And it can’t turn the app into a store for other apps.

Google Play’s Device and Network Abuse policy starts from a stricter position. Apps may not update themselves outside Google Play or download executable code such as dex, JAR, or .so files from anywhere else. The policy then makes an exception for code that runs in an interpreter or virtual machine with only indirect access to Android APIs, and gives “JavaScript in a webview or browser” as its example. That code still can’t be used to break any other Play policy.

So both stores end up in the same place. Bug fixes, copy changes, UI tweaks, and incremental improvements to the app people already installed are fine. Using OTA to turn the app into something other than what was reviewed is not, and it puts your developer account at risk. Signed releases help with the security side of Apple’s conditions, and keeping your native versions disciplined keeps native changes inside reviewed binaries, where they belong.

A lot of OTA services only come as a hosted product. Patch can be either.

The server, release worker, and dashboard run on your infrastructure as a single Docker Compose deployment: Caddy for TLS, the Patch server, PostgreSQL, and S3-compatible object storage, with Cloudflare or CloudFront in front if you want a CDN. Your bundles, metrics, and release history stay on your network. The Capacitor SDK talks to the standard Patch server without any changes, so you set up the server once with the self-hosting guide, and cmpatch-capacitor handles everything Capacitor-specific from there.

The SDKs and CLIs are licensed under Apache 2.0. The server uses the Codemagic Server License, which is free for up to 1,000,000 monthly active devices and converts to Apache 2.0 two years after each release. The only thing you can’t do is resell Patch as a competing OTA service.

To try it before provisioning anything, run the local evaluation stack. It runs the real server, database, storage, and dashboard on your machine in Docker, and the Capacitor CLI can point straight at it:

The local server has a prefilled one-click login, so there’s no account to create.

Self-hosting makes the most sense for teams with strict data residency rules, regulated or air-gapped environments, or a preference for owning their infrastructure.

A free license doesn’t make infrastructure free. Somebody has to keep the server patched, look after the database, manage TLS and the CDN, and be on call when a release goes wrong. Plenty of teams would rather put that time into their app.

Hosted Patch runs the same software on our infrastructure. The first 100,000 monthly active users are free, there are no limits on updates or bandwidth, and the rest of the pricing is on our pricing page. Larger teams can get enterprise plans, dedicated servers, and geolocated servers that keep update infrastructure and data in a specific region.

Email sales@codemagic.io to talk about it.

The Patch documentation covers setup step by step, so this is an overview of the path from nothing to your first OTA release.

1. Decide where Patch runs. Self-host with the self-hosting guide, or talk to our team about hosted service. For a first look, the local stack above is enough.

2. Install the CLI and create one Patch app per platform. Each app comes with Staging and Production deployments, each with its own deployment key. Don’t let iOS and Android share a deployment. A release’s delivery path doesn’t include the platform, so the two would overwrite each other.

3. Add the SDK to your Capacitor project. It supports the two most recent Capacitor major versions (currently 7 and 8) and Android minSdkVersion 24 or higher.

Configuration goes in capacitor.config.ts, with one block per platform. The API URL and download base URL come from your Patch server: the self-host installer prints both, and we give them to you for hosted Patch.

Then call start() once the app has rendered its first screen:

Where you call it matters. start() is what tells the SDK the running bundle is healthy, so call it after your UI is actually up, not early in bootstrap. That way an update that crashes during startup still gets rolled back. Two more tips: every config value can also be set as a native resource (Info.plist or strings.xml) if you inject per-environment values in CI, and npx codemagic-patch-check-config is worth adding to your native build workflow to catch a shared deployment key before it ships. The check reads JSON only, so if your config is capacitor.config.ts, run it after npx cap sync and point it at the synced copy: npx codemagic-patch-check-config android/app/src/main/assets/capacitor.config.json. The Patch docs cover native setup for Capacitor, checking for updates, install modes, and the step-by-step APIs, and the SDK reference lists everything the SDK exports. Pick Capacitor in the switcher at the top of the docs menu to see the Capacitor version of each page.

4. Publish a release to Staging from the CLI. Build the web assets the way you already do, then publish that folder once per platform. --target-binary-version has to be the native version you will ship in the next step (CFBundleShortVersionString on iOS, versionName on Android). www below is the webDir from capacitor.config.ts.

Each command publishes one platform. Install a build that includes the SDK and uses that same native version if you want to try the Staging release on a device before it goes to the stores.

5. Ship the native release, then publish Production from CI. The SDK has to be in the installed app before a device can receive an update, so this first binary is a normal store release. Build, sign, and publish it through Codemagic as usual. CI/CD for Ionic apps walks through connecting the repo and a first workflow, and the Ionic Capacitor build guide covers code signing, versioning, and publishing for both platforms.

After that, Production releases belong in CI. Create a token with cmpatch-capacitor token create, store it with your server URL and the deployment IDs from deployment list, and publish from the pipeline. The first release guide covers that workflow, including promotion and staged rollouts.

Most Appflow concepts carry over directly. Appflow channels become Patch deployments, and you get Staging and Production from the start. A few things work differently, and it’s better to know about them before you start:

None of these should stop you, but the first one decides your timeline. The Appflow migration guide walks through the swap.

If you’re already using our CodePush service with cap-codepush, nothing changes for you today. When you’re ready, the move to Patch follows the same pattern: one native release with the new SDK, then you publish with cmpatch-capacitor instead of code-push.

We’d rather you choose the right tool than the wrong one from us, so here are the cases where Patch won’t help much.

Most of your changes are native. Plugin upgrades, Capacitor version bumps, and native features all need a reviewed binary whichever OTA service you use. For teams like that, a fast and reliable native build-and-publish setup matters more, and Codemagic handles that too.

Your beta program depends on runtime channel switching. The Patch Capacitor SDK doesn’t offer it today. Separate beta builds work, but it’s a different workflow, so think it through before migrating.

Your native versioning is a mess and you can’t fix it. Exact-version targeting will feel strict. We think strict is the safer default, because it makes the compatibility boundary visible instead of guessing at it, but it does ask for some discipline.

You’re happy on Appflow right now. You don’t have to move tomorrow. You do have to move before the end of 2027, and the native release the swap requires means you should start well before that.

No. Capacitor does not ship an updater. Codemagic Patch is a separate SDK, @codemagic/capacitor-patch, and a CLI, cmpatch-capacitor.

It can replace Appflow Live Updates for web-layer releases. Appflow shuts down on December 31, 2027, and the Patch SDK has to ship inside a native binary well before that, because devices still on the old SDK keep calling Appflow.

You can self-host the server for free for up to 1,000,000 monthly active devices. Hosted Patch is for companies above that, and you arrange it with us. There is no signup.

HTML, CSS, and JavaScript in the web layer can go out over the air, targeted at one exact native version. Plugin changes, native code, and native config still need a store release with a bumped version.

Capacitor is the simplest framework we’ve built OTA support for, and it now has its own Patch SDK and CLI, with binary diffs, automatic crash-loop rollback, signed releases, and staged rollouts with promotion, plus checks for the mistakes that most often turn into blank screens. You can run Patch yourself, free for up to a 1M monthly active users (MAU), or have us host it, with a free tier available for under 100k MAU. Enterprise plans offer dedicated or geolocated servers, and engineers who’ll work through your compliance requirements with you. Together with the Capacitor build, signing, and publishing support Codemagic already has, that covers the whole release process on one platform.

This is the first release of the Capacitor SDK and CLI (v0.1.0). The Patch release notes have the full changelog, and we’d love to hear how it works for you.

If Appflow’s shutdown is on your roadmap, start before it becomes urgent. Spin up the local evaluation stack this week, and put the SDK in your next native release.

#9640. Feds Suspect Ransom Negotiator Ran ShinyHunters Extortion Site

U.S. federal investigators pursuing the ShinyHunters hacking group that recently stole highly sensitive data from the FBI have identified executives at two different ransomware negotiation firms who maintained unusually close relations with the extortion group, KrebsOnSecurity has learned. Sources close to the investigation say one of the executives in the United States even helped ShinyHunters operate a website that pressured victims into paying a ransom.

Hackers aligned with ShinyHunters have claimed credit for dozens of major data breaches since 2019, when the group was primarily operated by cybercriminals living in France. As those original members were arrested or jailed one by one, control over the ShinyHunters brand eventually passed to “Rey,” identified last year as a teenage hacker from Amman, Jordan. According to the FBI, ShinyHunters has extorted more than $70 million from victims so far this year.

In late September, ShinyHunters hacked the FBI recruitment website fbijobs.gov and taunted the agency by threatening to publish the stolen files, which reportedly included medical and psychological records, Social Security numbers and home addresses, and information about each employee’s unit and specialization.

The FBI jobs site hack has prompted the agency to move with uncommon speed to arrest, detain and question people who had any communications with Rey or other ShinyHunters suspects. Reuters reported on October 3 that Rey had been detained by Jordanian authorities and was cooperating with the FBI.

Rey was able to assume control over the hacking group because one of its alleged senior members had just been nabbed. On the evening of September 15, 2026, authorities in the Netherlands arrested convicted hacker and ShinyHunters suspect Pepijn van der Stap. Dutch police reportedly used flash-bang grenades in an effort to stun and apprehend Van der Stap as he was logged in to various online accounts.

According to a source close to the investigation, the authorities arrested Van der Stap while he was using his Signal instant messaging account, which allowed them to read recent communications with frequent contacts — including ransomware negotiators based in Canada and the United States.

Multiple sources with knowledge of the matter told KrebsOnSecurity that Van der Stap’s messages were the key to unraveling a murder-for-hire plot that emerged immediately following his arrest. The Dutch news outlet RTL reported last month the two murders were allegedly to be committed abroad, and that there are indications Van der Stap gave the order for the attacks (there is no indication those orders were ever carried out).

On October 9, KrebsOnSecurity broke the news that the FBI arrested a 54-year-old Canadian cybersecurity executive named Edward Dubrovsky in connection with the ShinyHunters investigation. Dubrovsky, who recently published a book on handling cyber extortion that recommended always engaging with the hackers, was charged with threatening to disclose stolen or hacked data and interfering with interstate commerce through extortion, according to court records. Politico reports prosecutors have asked that Dubrovsky remain in custody pending trial, and that records related to his case remain under seal.

A source close to the investigation told KrebsOnSecurity that Van der Stap’s Signal messages showed he had frequent conversations with Mr. Dubrovsky and with at least one executive at a large U.S.-based consulting firm, and that these executives often knew the details about new ShinyHunters victims before the victims themselves had even learned of the breach.

That source shared another potentially explosive finding by federal investigators: the Dutch hacker’s chats showed Mr. Dubrovsky knew ShinyHunters had stolen highly sensitive data from FBI servers, and that he never informed the bureau of the data breach prior to ShinyHunters threatening on Twitter/X to publish the agency’s deeply personal personnel files.

KrebsOnSecurity has learned from two sources close to the ShinyHunters probe that FBI investigators believe at least one executive at a U.S.-based consulting firm played an active role in operating the now-defunct ShinyHunters victim extortion website “shinywire[.]com.” KrebsOnSecurity is not naming the U.S. company or the suspected executive(s) for now because they have not yet been charged with a crime, but it is a prestigious firm with more than 1,000 associates.

A section of the homepage for the now-defunct Shinywire website.

The Shinywire website was active from approximately May 3, 2026 until October 16 and had entries for nearly 100 organizations hacked by ShinyHunters. Each entry urged victims to engage with the cybercrime group and discuss terms for payment. The pages also included samples of stolen files and promised those files would be published online if the victim ignored their demands.

The following screenshot shows a cached portion of the Shinywire extortion page for Intuitive Surgical, an American medical technology company that was breached in March 2026 after an employee fell for a targeted phishing email.

The Shinywire website, as indexed by urlscan.io. This listing is an extortion demand targeting Intuitive Surgical, an American medical technology company breached in March 2026 by a targeted phishing email attack that compromised an employee’s credentials.

Victim organizations that refused to engage or negotiate after seven days would find all of their stolen data published on the ShinyHunters victim shaming blog (a website that is only reachable via the anonymity network Tor).

In a story published October 15, The Globe and Mail wrote that a few months before Edward Dubrovsky was arrested by the FBI, the Canadian cybersecurity executive alleged in court documents he had become collateral damage in a campaign by a former business partner to “destroy” another industry executive.

The story noted that Dubrovsky filed the lawsuit in Ontario this year against Daniel Tobok, the former chief executive of Cypfer, a cybersecurity firm founded in Toronto with offices in the U.S., Britain, the Netherlands, the United Arab Emirates, and Mexico. The two first became business partners in 2017 and later developed Cypfer together, where Mr. Dubrovsky was a managing partner and chief operating officer. But by 2024, the two had a falling out, with Dubrovsky accusing Tobok of gradually excluding him from business matters and making “increasingly capricious business decisions.”

Mr. Tobok reportedly denied the allegations and filed a counterclaim, accusing Mr. Dubrovsky of accessing confidential information and unfairly competing with Cypfer through work at another firm called CyberSteward Inc. He also said Mr. Dubrovsky has misrepresented himself as a Cypfer founder, and is not a shareholder.

According to interviews with several former colleagues of Mr. Tobok, as far back as eight years ago he was known to ransomware purveyors by a particular nickname: Ghostbyte. In 2018, a Canadian company was hacked by Dharma, a prolific Russian-language ransomware affiliate program that first surfaced in 2016. The victim company told the Dharma ransomware representative they were leaning toward paying because some of the files were unrecoverable after being locked, but that they needed a better guarantee that Dharma would keep their word if paid.

A redacted copy of the Dharma rep’s reply is pictured below, and it shows the ransomware group urged the victim to contact a person at a Canadian IT firm that helps companies seeking such guarantees. The Dharma rep recommended the victim contact the email address ghostbyte@tutanota.com.

“If you want guarantees, you can write to the IT company,” the Dharma reply advised. “Take the phone and negotiate with them. This IT company often solves such problems in Canada. You can contact them and sign a contract for services. You’ll still have to pay.”

An email reply from the Dharma ransomware group to a victim, recommending they contact an email address that is connected to Mr. Tobok.

It’s unclear if Mr. Tobok ever used that Ghostbyte address offered by the Dharma representative, and he has not responded to multiple requests for comment. However, the breach tracking service Constella Intelligence finds an email address Mr. Tobok has frequently used — dtobok@me.com — is associated with two online accounts where the chosen username was “ghostbyte,” including a Snapchat account.

Incidentally, Constella also finds the Dharma rep’s email address luckygoodlucky@tuta.io is associated with a cryptocurrency address that processed 38 transactions totaling 43 bitcoin, ~$3.5 million at today’s value (the most recent transaction for this wallet is dated February 2019).

In a statement shared on October 14, Cypfer said the company’s business does not include making or facilitating ransomware payments, and that Cypfer learned of Dubrovsky’s arrest when the news first broke in the media.

“We had no prior knowledge of Mr. Dubrovsky’s arrest,” a spokesperson told KrebsOnSecurity via email. “CYPFER has not received any outreach from law enforcement and, to our knowledge, is not the target of any law enforcement investigation.”

The statement said CyberSteward and Cypfer are separate companies with no officers, directors or employees in common, and that Cypfer was recently acquired by the Apros Group, a holding company led by Jason Hogg, a former FBI special agent and former CEO of Aon Cyber Solutions Group. In 2020, Aon aquired Cytelligence, a security consulting firm where Mr. Tobok was founder and CEO and Mr. Dubrovsky was a managing partner.

It is not illegal in the United States to pay hackers for an encryption key to unlock servers infected with ransomware, or in exchange for a promise to delete any stolen files and refrain from publishing them online. While victim organizations can land in legal hot water if they pay a ransom to a group that is sanctioned by the U.S. Treasury Department, ShinyHunters is not among the ransomware groups currently sanctioned by the United States or by any other government.

Experts say ransomware victims are typically directed by their insurance provider to work with a specific incident response firm. But not all cyber forensics and breach response companies will agree to facilitate payments to ransomware groups on behalf of their clients. As a result, once victim firms make a decision to pay, the firms that eschew rewarding extortionists are invariably replaced by companies that have no such qualms.

In December 2024, ShinyHunters began extorting the education technology company PowerSchool, stealing private information on 62 million students and 9.5 million teachers in the U.S. and Canada. PowerSchool reportedly paid a $2.85 million ransom demand, and a “frequently asked questions” statement (PDF) about the breach says PowerSchool was assisted in that effort by CyberSteward (ShinyHunters affiliate Matthew Lane, 20, of Sterling, Mass., was sentenced in November 2025 to four years in prison for his admitted role in the PowerSchool hack).

But that ransom payment did not stop future extortion attempts using the same stolen data. By May 2025, individual school districts were reportedly receiving separate ransom demands using samples of the same stolen files. While nobody has alleged ShinyHunters was behind the second wave of extortion against PowerSchool users, the incident drives home the reality that there is no technical way to verify the threat actors have deleted the stolen data as promised, or prevent others from abusing the same records.

A number of leading cyber incident response firms, including Coveware and Unit 221B, have consistently warned victims against paying ShinyHunters, noting that “destroyed” victim data is often kept, resold or used to extort the company’s clients directly later on.

The FBI echoed those sentiments in an alert on May 15, 2026 advising victims against paying the ShinyHunters group. Meanwhile, ShinyHunters members have been harassing and threatening employees at Coveware and Unit 221B for offering this advice.

The following screenshots show just how annoyed the ShinyHunters leaders were with Coveware’s relentless advice against paying the group. The first image is from a conversation on May 6, 2026 that took place between the group’s main account on Telegram and a co-conspirator. In that chat, snippets of which were shared with KrebsOnSecurity by a trusted source, ShinyHunters complained that Coveware was harming the group’s payment rates.

The operator of the ShinyHunters account on Telegram speaking privately with a co-conspirator and complaining that Coveware was harming their business.

“Go on my website, majority of those companies would’ve paid if it weren’t for Coveware giving them misinformation,” the ShinyHunters account wrote. “Someone (100% Coveware) is going out of their way to make sure i am not paid.”

In another conversation on April 11, 2026, the ShinyHunters Telegram account privately said they were trying to “eliminate the problem,” which they said was Coveware. Coveware declined to comment for this story.

“I’m sure the company will pay but in this specific case I am aware of Coveware and their involvement, and I’ve probably been not getting a lot of other negotiations mostly likely because Coveware keeps getting involved,” the ShinyHunters account bemoaned.

The operator of the ShinyHunters account on Telegram telling a co-conspirator they were “trying to eliminate the problem,” which they identified as Coveware advising victims not to pay the cybercrime group.

Mark Camillo is chief executive at CyberAcuView, an industry group founded in 2021 by a consortium of major cyber insurance carriers. Camillo said some firms charge a flat retainer fee, while those that specialize in helping companies negotiate a ransom payment tend to charge a percentage of the total ransom amount paid.

That latter dynamic, he said, is an inherent conflict of interest, as the negotiator has every incentive to make things more favorable to the attackers because they are financially incentivized to negotiate and pay out, and to not negotiate down on the price.

“It has come to the industry’s attention that many of the ransomware payers charge a percentage of the final payment which may or may not be disclosed,” Camillo said. “This makes no sense if they are also the negotiator. There needs to be more transparency in the process as no one in the ecosystem should be profiting purely on the size of the ransomware transaction or payment itself.”

Camillo said the firms doing this work would argue the fees are needed because there may be unexpectedly higher costs to secure larger quantities of cryptocurrency or more risk carrying the float, and because cryptocurrency exchanges may charge higher fees for high risk transactions.

“There definitely needs to be more visibility around the transaction and clarity on the increasing value of the crypto and the exchange’s percent in the transaction to get to the bottom of this and remove any misaligned incentives,” he said.

In recent months, the U.S. Department of Justice has prosecuted a number of ransomware negotiators alleged to have conspired with cybercriminals to defraud their clients. On October 7, the DOJ charged MonsterCloud CEO Zohar Pinhasi, 50, with wire fraud and conspiracy for allegedly charging customers to remediate ransomware attacks without paying the hackers. According to charging documents, Pinhasi secretly went behind his customers’ backs and paid hackers anyway, paying ransomware groups $8 million while charging customers $19 million.

In July, Angelo Martino, a 41-year-old ransomware negotiator from Land O’Lakes, Florida, was sentenced to 70 months in prison for conspiring with the Blackcat/ALPHV ransomware group to extort multiple victims. According to the DOJ, Martino was paid by BlackCat attackers to provide confidential information about the negotiating position and strategy of his employer’s clients and enable the ransomware actors to maximize the ransoms paid by the victims.

#9639. Most Frequently Asked Questions About Email Marketing


1. Why is email marketing important?

Email is the marketing tool that helps you  create a seamless, connected, frictionless buyer journey. More importantly, email marketing allows you to build relationships with prospects, customers, and past customers. It's your chance to speak  to them right in their inbox, at a time that suits them. Along with the right message, email can become one of your most powerful marketing channels.

2. What is benefits of email marketing?

Email marketing is best way for creating long term relationship with your clients, and increasing sales in our company.

Benefits of email marketing for bussiness:
  • Better brand recognition
  • Statistics of what works best
  • More sales
  • Targeted audience
  • More traffic to your products/services/newsletter
  • Build credibility
Most  bussinesses are using email marketing and making tons of money with email marketing.

3. What is the simplest day and time to send my marketing emails?


Again, the answer to this question varies from company to company. And again, testing is the way to find out what works best. Typically, weekends and mornings seem to be  times when multiple emails are opened, but since your audience may have different habits, it's best to experiment and then use your  data to decide.

 4. Which metrics should I be looking at?


The two most important metrics for email marketing are  open rate and click-through rate. If your emails aren't opened, subscribers will never see your full marketing message, and if they open them but don't click through to your site, your emails won't convert.

5. How do I write a decent subject line?


The best subject lines are short and to the point, accurately describing  the content of the email, but also catchy and intriguing, so the reader wants to know more. Once Again, this is the perfect place for  A/B testing, to see what types of subject lines work best with your audience. Your call to action should be clear and  simple. It should be somewhere at the top of your email for those who haven't finished reading the entire email,  then repeated  at the end for those reading all the way through. It should state exactly what you want subscribers to do, for example "Click here to download the premium theme for free.




6. Is email marketing still effective?

Email marketing is one of the most effective ways for a business to reach its customers directly. Think about it. You don't post something on your site  hoping people will visit it. You don't even post something on a social media page and hope fans  see it. You're sending something straight to each person's inbox, where they'll definitely  see it! Even if they don't open it, they'll still see your subject line and business name every time you send an email, so you're still communicating directly with your audience.



7. However do I grow my email subscribers list? Should i buy an email list or build it myself?

Buying an email list is  waste of time & money. These email accounts are unverified and not interested in your brand. The mailing list is useless if your subscribers do not open your emails. There are different ways to grow your mailing list. 

Give them a free ebook and host it on a landing page where they have to enter the email to download the file and also create a forum page on your website, asks your visitors what questions they might have about your business, and collects email addresses to follow up with them.


8. How do I prevent audience from unsubscribing?


If the  subject line of the email is irrelevant to  customers, they will ignore it multiple times. But, if it keeps repeating, they are intercepted and unsubscribed from your emails. So, send relevant emails for the benefit of the customer. Don't send emails that often only focus  on sales, offers and discounts. 
Submit information about your business and offers so you can connect with customers. You can also update them on recent trends in your industry. The basic role of an email is first and foremost to  connect with customers, get the most out of this tool.

9. What is the difference between a cold email and a spam email?


Cold emails are mostly sales emails that are sent with content align to the needs of the recipient. It is usually personalized and includes a business perspective. However, it is still an unsolicited email. And all unsolicited emails are marked as SPAM. 
Regularly receiving this type of unsolicited email in your users' inboxes, chances are  your emails will soon be diverted to  spam or junk folders. The most important thing to prevent this from happening is to respect your recipients' choice to opt-out of receiving emails from you. You can add the links to easily unsubscribe. You must be familiar with the CAN-SPAM Act and its regulations.

10. Where can I find email template?

Almost all email campaign tools provide you with ready-made templates. Whether you use MailChimp or Pardot, you'll get several email templates ready to use.
 However, if you want to create a template from scratch, you can do so.Most of email campaign tools have option to paste the HTML code of your own design. 


11. What email marketing trend will help marketers succeed in 2022?

Is it a trend to listen to  and get to know your customers? I think people realize how bad it feels for a brand or a company to obsess over themselves without knowing their customers personal needs. People who listen empathetically and then provide value based on what they learn will win.


Final Saying


 You can approach email marketing in different ways. We have compiled a list of most frequently asked questions to help you understand how to get started, what constraints you need to keep in mind, and what future development you will need, we don’t have 100% answers to every situation and there’s always a chance you will have something new and different to deal with as you market your own business.

#9638. Google, Partners Disrupt 1.3 Million-Device-Strong XCPE Botnet

Google alleges that Android device manufacturer Videostrong ran the operation, which infected set-top boxes and IoT devices with a backdoor to create infrastructure for criminal activity.

Google and industry partners disrupted the XCPE botnet, a cybercriminal operation that planted a backdoor in more than 1.3 million Android-based set-top boxes, turning consumer devices into infrastructure for malicious activity.

The operation, attributed with "high confidence" by Google's Threat Intelligence Group (GTIG) to Android device manufacturer Videostrong Technology Co., involved deliberately embedding the XCPE backdoor malware in multiple device models and brands since at least 2024, according to a blog post published earlier this week by GTIG.

Rather than simply exploiting vulnerable devices, however, the manufacturer allegedly built a system that allowed criminal affiliates to access compromised hardware and deploy their own malicious software, Google said.

"Videostrong monetized the backdoor by selling access to criminal affiliates and loading those affiliates' malware modules onto infected devices," according to the post. "These secondary modules were conducting ad-fraud; silently enrolling infected devices into residential proxy networks; and loading additional malware onto XCPE-compromised devices."

Related:'Aokigahara' Stealer Targets 'Developer Keyrings' & AI Assistants

Google and its partners, which included Japan's National Police Agency, Lumen, HUMAN Security, Plume, Synthient, and TrendAI, took legal action against Videostrong to disrupt the domains and servers it used to control the botnet, install affiliate malware modules, and operate the command-and-control (C2) infrastructure used by those modules.

Because the affiliate modules "each have diversified distribution channels for their modules beyond XCPE," Google assessed that disrupting their C2 infrastructure "will sever access to at least 10 million additional compromised devices," according to the post.

Google has also cut ties with Videostrong and banned the manufacturer, along with any future subsidiaries or affiliates, from building or selling certified Android devices or supplying software to other certified vendors. Videostrong did not immediately return Dark Reading's request for comment on Wednesday.

Most devices infected by the XCPE botnet were Android TV set-top boxes. However, the botnet also included other Android-based IoT devices, including telehealth equipment, karaoke machines, and digital signage systems, according to Google.

This wider exposure of IoT devices is reflected in Bitdefender's "2026 IoT Security Landscape Report," released this week. The findings recorded 5.4 billion security events and 6.2 billion vulnerability observations across devices behind approximately 10.4 million monitored routers between January and September 2026. While these figures represent detected activity and identified device vulnerabilities rather than confirmed compromises, they underline the scale of the threat facing connected devices and the potential attack surface they present to businesses.

Related:BeyondTrust Remote Support Zero-Day Continues Trend of Exploited Edge Bugs

While most of Videostrong's interactions with victim devices involved installing, uninstalling, and configuring malware modules, operators also carried out so-called "sensitive actions," according to Google. These include capturing live screenshots; injecting keystrokes; exfiltrating sensitive information, such as account and device details, package inventories, and system logs; and executing shell scripts and commands, including those used to establish reverse shells on infected devices.

Although the operation primarily targeted consumer devices, it has significant security implications for businesses and enterprise organizations. XCPE demonstrates how compromised IoT equipment can be turned into criminal infrastructure, providing attackers with residential proxy networks that help conceal malicious activity, evade IP-based security controls, and facilitate fraud.

Related:EDR Evasion Stack Helps Process Injection Slip Past Defenses

"By turning 1.3 million devices into residential proxies, threat actors fuel the exact infrastructure used to attack high-value API endpoints," says Mark Mazur, field chief technology officer (CTO) for mobile application security firm Approov.

Because attacks launched through the botnet can originate from legitimate consumer IP addresses, standard security defenses such as geo-blocking, ASN blocking, and IP reputation filters "are practically useless against them," he says.

"They are creating infrastructure, largely based on IoT devices, that can power sophisticated credential stuffing and API abuse campaigns," Mazur adds.

The malware's ability to execute remote commands, conduct network reconnaissance, and maintain persistent access also raises concerns about connected devices deployed in corporate and healthcare environments. Digital signage, televisions, and telehealth equipment, for example, could provide attackers with an opportunity to explore networks or establish a foothold if compromised devices are connected to inadequately segmented networks. Google has not confirmed that any such activity has occurred, however.

Google requires original equipment manufacturers (OEMs) to undergo a comprehensive suite of compatibility and security tests to participate in the Android ecosystem. However, Videostrong was able to evade these checks by "employing obfuscation techniques" that exploited a weakness in the review process, according to Google. The malicious code was loaded after the device's first boot, allowing it to bypass the initial security checks.

Calling Videostrong's actions "an unacceptable breach of trust," Google said it has since strengthened its review processes to protect the integrity of Android TV firmware and "better safeguard against similar activity in the future," according to the post.

As an additional protective measure, Google encouraged consumers to be wary of applications offering payment in exchange for "unused bandwidth" or "sharing your Internet," as these could turn their set-top boxes and other IoT products into part of a residential proxy network.

"These applications are primary ways for illicit proxy networks to grow, and could open security vulnerabilities on the device's home network," according to the post.

Google also urged Android users to stick to trusted app stores, review the permissions requested by third-party VPN and proxy applications, and ensure built-in security protections such as Google Play Protect are active.

Finally, Google called on mobile platforms, ISPs, online marketplaces, and other technology providers to continue sharing threat intelligence and implementing security best practices to identify malicious backdoors, illicit proxy networks, and other harmful software to prevent similar botnet operations from emerging in the future.

Elizabeth Montalbano is freelance writer, editor, and journalist with 30 years of professional experience and a master's degree from Arizona State University. Her areas of expertise include enterprise technology, cybersecurity, business, and culture. During her long career, Elizabeth has lived and worked as a full-time journalist in Phoenix, San Francisco, and New York City. She specializes in news coverage and analysis, using her years of experience to look at the current state of cybersecurity with a critical gaze. She currently resides in a village on the southwest coast of Portugal, where in her free time she enjoys surfing, hiking with her dogs, growing plants, and playing and performing as a singer and musician.

#9637. Understanding Software PLCs: Architecture, Execution, and Security Boundaries

Security researcher focused on Industrial Control Systems (ICS), protocol forensics, and open-source security tools.

Security researcher focused on Industrial Control Systems (ICS), protocol forensics, and open-source security tools.

Security researcher focused on Industrial Control Systems (ICS), protocol forensics, and open-source security tools.

When I finished my industrial protocol research series, I wanted to move closer to the systems using those protocols. I turned my attention to software PLCs and started investigating OpenPLC Runtime v4.

My first investigation quickly took me into runtime internals and the Linux environment supporting them. There was a lot to learn, but I eventually realised that I was spending more time understanding implementation details than answering the security questions I had originally set out to explore.

I stepped back and reorganised the project. Before investigating how software PLCs could be attacked, I wanted to understand what they actually are, how they operate, and how their different components fit together. That became Part I: Software PLC Foundations.

A Programmable Logic Controller (PLC) is an industrial computing system responsible for monitoring inputs, executing control logic, and controlling outputs connected to a physical process. It receives information from devices such as sensors, evaluates that information against its programmed instructions, and sends commands to equipment such as motors, pumps, and valves.

Traditionally, PLC functionality has been delivered through dedicated industrial controller hardware. A typical controller brings together a CPU, memory, system software, communication interfaces, and connections to industrial I/O. Depending on the platform, these components may be integrated into a compact unit or arranged as a modular system.

A Software PLC (SoftPLC) implements the same fundamental control functionality through a software runtime operating on a compatible computing platform. That platform might be an industrial PC, an embedded computer, or another supported computing environment.

This contrast became the starting point for my first investigation. A software PLC still relies on physical hardware. What changes is how the controller functionality is implemented and how it relates to the underlying computing environment.

In a traditional PLC, the manufacturer generally delivers the controller as an integrated platform with its own firmware, execution environment, and supported hardware interfaces. In a SoftPLC, the runtime depends more directly on the host platform. The operating environment supplies computing resources and system services, while the runtime provides the environment for loading and executing the control application.

That separation introduces some interesting possibilities. Software PLCs can offer more flexibility in hardware selection and integration with other software systems. It also means that the host operating environment becomes part of the controller's architecture and something we need to understand when examining its security.

The deployment model adds another layer to this picture.

A software PLC can run directly on a host operating system, use a real-time operating environment, or operate inside a virtual machine or container. These arrangements are quite different. A virtual machine provides a guest operating system over virtualised hardware managed by a hypervisor. A container packages and isolates application processes while sharing the host operating system's kernel.

That difference is important. The isolation provided by a container is not the same as the separation between a virtual machine and its host. Access to devices, network interfaces, filesystems, and host resources also depends on how the environment is configured.

I also wanted to understand the assumptions around execution timing. There is a tendency to associate deterministic control exclusively with dedicated PLC hardware, as though running control software on a general-purpose platform automatically makes predictable execution impossible. The reality is more dependent on the complete configuration. Processor resources, scheduling, operating system behaviour, runtime implementation, I/O handling, and competing workloads all influence execution timing.

Virtualisation does not automatically rule out predictable execution either. Research examining virtual PLC implementations has demonstrated that comparable timing behaviour is achievable under particular tested configurations. That does not mean every virtualised deployment will meet every industrial timing requirement. The intended application and the complete system still have to be considered.

There is also the physical environment to account for. An ordinary computer running PLC software should not automatically be treated as equivalent to industrial-rated controller equipment. Environmental conditions, supported interfaces, power requirements, and equipment qualification remain relevant.

By this point, the contrast between a hardware PLC and a SoftPLC was becoming much clearer. I could also see why identifying the deployment environment was important before making assumptions about the security of a particular implementation.

The computing platform provides somewhere for the PLC runtime to operate, but the runtime needs a control application to execute.

Industrial control applications are commonly developed using the programming languages defined by IEC 61131-3. These include Structured Text (ST), Ladder Diagram (LD), and Function Block Diagram (FBD), alongside Sequential Function Chart (SFC) elements used to organise sequential operations.

The languages provide different ways of expressing control behaviour. Structured Text uses a textual syntax, Ladder Diagram represents logic through graphical electrical-style elements, and Function Block Diagram connects functional blocks to describe operations. SFC provides a way to organise sequences through steps and transitions.

The standard also defines how control applications can be organised through Program Organization Units (POUs). Programs, functions, and function blocks provide different building blocks for structuring application logic. A function block, for example, can retain internal state between executions, which makes it useful for representing operations that need to remember previous conditions.

Understanding these structures helped me move beyond thinking of a PLC program as one large block of instructions. A control application can contain several interconnected pieces of logic, each contributing to the behaviour of the overall system.

There is also a process between writing that logic and having it run on a controller. This is where the engineering lifecycle becomes important.

An engineering workstation is used to develop and configure the application. Depending on the platform, the project may then pass through compilation or code generation before being transferred to the target PLC runtime. The runtime loads the resulting application and makes it available for execution.

The engineering environment often remains involved after deployment. Engineers may use it to monitor variables, inspect controller status, modify application logic, or perform online changes where the platform supports them. Projects also need to be backed up, maintained, and recovered when something goes wrong.

I found this part particularly important because the engineering project, generated application, and program currently loaded on the controller are related, but they are not necessarily identical artefacts. Platform-specific compilation, project formats, libraries, and deployment procedures all affect how an application moves through its lifecycle.

Interchange standards such as IEC 61131-10 also address the exchange of PLC project information using XML. That provides a basis for exchanging engineering data, although it does not guarantee that projects will behave identically across different runtimes and vendor environments.

Once the application reaches the runtime, another important contrast appears: how the program is executed.

A familiar PLC execution pattern is the scan cycle. The controller reads input states, evaluates the control logic, and updates outputs before repeating the cycle. This provides a useful way to understand basic PLC operation, although actual execution models vary. Some platforms support multiple tasks with different priorities, intervals, or triggering conditions.

The runtime is responsible for coordinating this execution according to its implementation and configuration. Timing requirements become especially important here. A control application that produces the correct logical result may still be unsuitable for its intended process if it cannot execute within the required time.

This also explains why runtime scheduling, resource availability, and watchdog mechanisms matter. They contribute to how the controller behaves during normal operation and how it responds when execution does not proceed as expected.

Taken together, the programming model, engineering workflow, and execution environment describe how control logic travels from an engineering project into a running industrial controller. They also reveal several points where the integrity and availability of that application matter.

By the time I reached the final investigation, the different pieces of the architecture were starting to connect.

A software PLC depends on its host platform. The host supports the runtime, the runtime executes the control application, and the application interacts with the industrial process through supported I/O and communication interfaces. The engineering environment provides another route through which the application is created, configured, and maintained.

Each relationship establishes a boundary worth examining.

At the platform level, operating system privileges, user accounts, filesystem permissions, and process isolation influence what the runtime and its supporting services can access. Where containers or virtual machines are involved, their configuration introduces additional isolation boundaries and dependencies.

At the application level, the integrity of the control program matters because its instructions determine how the controller responds to the process. The engineering workstation and program deployment workflow therefore deserve attention alongside the runtime itself. An assessment that only looks at the PLC host can miss important parts of how control logic is developed and delivered.

The communication side introduces another set of considerations. Management interfaces may support configuration, monitoring, and program deployment, while industrial communication interfaces allow the controller to exchange data with other systems. These interfaces have different purposes and may have different security requirements.

Availability also deserves attention. A software PLC may share processor time, memory, storage, and other resources with services running on the same host. Depending on the deployment, resource pressure or failure of a supporting component could affect runtime operation.

This is where the six investigations came together for me. The security boundaries of a software PLC cannot be understood by looking at the runtime in isolation. They emerge from the relationship between the deployment environment, the control application, the engineering process, and the interfaces connecting the system to its surroundings.

I used standards, manufacturer documentation, academic publications, and implementation documentation throughout Part I. OpenPLC Runtime v4 served as a useful practical reference when I needed to examine how some of these architectural ideas appear in an actual implementation. I kept its specific design separate from general SoftPLC concepts, since one implementation cannot represent every platform.

I also tried to keep documented behaviour, observations from the lab, and my own technical interpretations distinct. That contrast is important when drawing security conclusions. An exposed interface or a process running with elevated privileges can be relevant to an investigation, but its presence alone does not establish a vulnerability or demonstrate what an attacker can achieve.

The goal of this first part was to establish the system context needed to ask better security questions.

With Part I complete, the research moves into Part II: Attack Techniques.

The next stage will examine established techniques involving PLC program and configuration tampering, runtime manipulation, and execution disruption. The focus will be on understanding what these techniques can achieve against software PLC environments and gathering evidence of their actual impact.

The work from Part I gives me a much better starting point for those investigations. I also intend to retain and use the earlier OpenPLC implementation work wherever it helps answer a relevant security question.

This article brings together the main ideas from Part I, but there's more behind it. I've documented the individual investigations, technical details, diagrams, and supporting material in the project repository.

You can explore the research on GitHub: 404saint/softplc-security-research.

Inside the PLC Runtime: What OpenPLC v4 Reveals About Its Linux Environment

#9636. Granite Switch 4.1.1 — Update models like you update software

Just over a week ago, we released Granite Switch 4.1, showing that our modular Switch architecture lets you configure a language model with specialized, cache-efficient adapters — adding new expertise on a single endpoint.

Granite Switch 4.1.1 is a patch release. The version number means what it means in software: fully backwards compatible with 4.1, no migration, incremental improvements under the hood.

While we are excited about these new features, what is notable is the speed and efficiency with which our teams could release this update. Apart from training the new ASR model and Decision adapter, nothing was recomputed: the base model is untouched. You compose the latest adapters you want and deploy.

This pattern can power far more than patch releases to an IBM-provided model. We're working on tutorials and an Adapter SDK so developers and third-party providers can build their own adapters — iterate on versions, test features, and ship updates the way you ship software. More soon.

Until then, test out our latest models, and try out the new multilingual and punctuation capabilities powering our Speech-to-Decisions demo.

#9635. Widespread PHP Flaw May Cause Many Site Outages Today

Expect to see quite a few websites serving error pages today: Nearly 70 percent of websites need to update their core software to fix a pair of vulnerabilities that allow an attacker to seize full control over affected servers. Experts say there are working exploits for the flaws, and that these critical bugs are already being exploited in the wild.

The flaws at issue are present in PHP, the programming language that powers sites running on a large number of web publishing systems, including Drupal, Magento, Joomla and WordPress. Earlier today, PHP released an emergency security update to fix two critical bugs that can allow an attacker to execute code of their choosing on a vulnerable server.

Reuters reports that government websites in Europe and elsewhere went offline today after the PHP vulnerabilities were disclosed. Cloudflare said it has already detected some exploitation of the flaw, and that at 3:02 am (UTC) it implemented web application firewall rules to protect websites from attack traffic seeking to exploit the bugs, which could cause a denial of service condition, remote code execution, and data exposure.

OpenAI, which was involved in the vulnerability research and outreach, said “given the severity of these flaws and PHP’s widespread use, we consider this one of the most impactful security issues in recent memory.”

Censys, a company that tracks the technology used by Internet hosts, said a recent scan identified approximately 2.58 million Internet facing hosts and 54.9 million web properties running PHP.

Security experts at Wiz said every PHP version released in the last decade is affected by at least one of these vulnerabilities [full disclosure: Wiz is an advertiser on this blog].

“These findings rank among the most severe vulnerabilities discovered in PHP, and arguably in software history,” reads a blog post published today by a team of researchers at Wiz, which was one of several organizations credited with discovering the vulnerabilities. “The underlying flaws had been present for decades, but demonstrating their exploitability required an exceptionally complex chain of steps, at the edge of what human researchers could practically achieve. Frontier AI models substantially reduced that barrier, turning a longstanding flaw into an exploit.”

The Wiz researchers say it is likely the PHP vulnerabilities will be mass-exploited to install web-based backdoors or “web shells,” which give attackers a web-based panel that allows them to remotely control infected sites. Wiz said that prior to the PHP bugs being publicly disclosed, the company worked with the PHP team, Calif and OpenAI to measure the size of the problem and coordinate patch verification and disclosure.

The PHP zero-day vulnerabilities are being tracked by their CVE numbers, CVE-2026-109618 and CVE-2026-109619, and they affect all web servers running PHP 5.4 or later. The bugs are fixed in PHP 8.5.12, 8.4.27, 8.3.36, and 8.2.35.

According to Wiz, PHP is so deeply embedded in many web applications that we are likely to see organizations struggling to patch these vulnerabilities for some time to come, comparing this PHP vulnerability pair with the Log4Shell weakness that emerged in 2021 — a widespread, severe-as-it-gets security flaw in Log4j, a popular Java logging framework.

“A vulnerability in core PHP reaches far beyond a single application,” the Wiz researchers wrote. “PHP runs across clouds, hosting providers, content-delivery networks and millions of independently managed servers. Reducing exposure before the technical details became public required coordinated work across that entire ecosystem.”

The SANS Internet Storm Center is keeping an eye on major software platforms that are shipping updates to deal with these PHP flaws. For example, Ubuntu just released updated PHP packages. For a technical deep-dive on these vulnerabilities that tells the timeline of the discovery of these bugs in a comic book style, check out this post from Calif, another technology company credited with finding the PHP flaws.

A snapshot of php2shell.censys.com, the website Censys set up to track the PHP vulnerabilities.

This is a fast-moving story. Updates will be noted here with timestamps.

Update, 2:30 pm ET: Add figures from Censys and a link to Calif’s writeup.

#9634. Critical Rails Bug Threatens to Derail Vulnerable Servers

An attacker could write arbitrary files and read sensitive files via images uploaded to the Rails Active Storage ImageMagick integration, possibly positioning a threat actor for lateral movement.

A critical vulnerability in Rails could send impacted Web servers off the tracks.

Rails, or Ruby on Rails, is a Web application framework built on Ruby. The framework's Active Storage component handles file uploads and can use the ImageMagick image processing suite to analyze uploaded images. And unfortunately, a flaw enables attackers to write arbitrary files to a Web server via ImageMagick.

The vulnerability (which is tracked as GHSA-f3w6-w445-fwh9) is critical, with a CVSS score of 9.8, and is considered so severe because an attacker could upload a crafted image file to write arbitrary files, read sensitive files, access secrets such as secret_key_base files, external system credentials, database passwords, and third-party tokens. These secrets could then be used for lateral movement or remote code execution into said external systems.

As a GitHub advisory published by the Rails maintainers explains, "A Rails application that processes attachments with ImageMagick may allow an unauthenticated attacker to write arbitrary files on the server and, when attachments are stored with the Disk service, to read arbitrary files readable by the application process."

Related:Undead Software Projects Continue to Raise Security Risks

The vulnerability exists because ImageMagick doesn't necessarily decide how to process a file (i.e., which coder it uses) based on the filename or extension, but rather on its contents. This means an attacker can upload an image file named "maliciousfile.jpeg" but contains content that causes ImageMagick to invoke a different coder. This can potentially allow arbitrary file reads or writes on the server.

Vulnerable versions of Active Storage include those 8.0 versions prior to 8.0.5.2 and 8.1 versions prior to 8.1.4.1. Those affected organizations running Rails applications that use ImageMagick for Active Storage image processing run with a security policy that does not block the affected coders, and accept uploads from untrusted users.

Active Storage patches are available now. The GitHub page includes further mitigation requirements for applications that use MiniMagick and ImageMagick.

Additionally, if an application stores attachments through the Disk service, users should "change secret_key_base and every secret readable by the application process, including the master key and everything config/credentials.yml.enc holds, storage and database credentials, and third-party tokens," the GitHub advisory said. Users should not retain exposed secrets as a fallback.

If a user requires a workaround, the GitHub page offers system rules the user can apply into ImageMagick's system policy.

Related:Claude Model Builds Exploits Across Major Browsers & OSes

Jake Knott, head of threat intelligence for exposure management vendor watchTowr, tells Dark Reading the firm has already reproduced the vulnerability in a lab environment, and "that against the right target, exploitation won't be difficult at all."

Moreover, he says he'd be surprised if public proof-of-concept exploit code took more than a few days to come to light.

"For attackers, reproducing the vulnerability here is likely the easy part, as the patterns and primitives involved in exploitation are well established," Knott says. "The hard part is finding software and deployments that are common enough, and configured in a vulnerable way, to deliver impact at scale indiscriminately."

At Dark Reading, he covers a variety of cybersecurity topics, including the cybercrime ecosystem, open source security, and the intersection between AI and threat actors. #9633. AI-search Results Are Emerging As An Important Influencer and Creator Discovery Tool

Jon Stojan is a professional writer based in Wisconsin committed to delivering diverse and exceptional content..

Jon Stojan is a professional writer based in Wisconsin committed to delivering diverse and exceptional content..

Jon Stojan is a professional writer based in Wisconsin committed to delivering diverse and exceptional content..

Until recently, creators and influencers could boost their visibility and their potential earnings by winning the search battleground on Instagram, TikTok, or Google. But a shift in search behavior is reshaping creator and influencer discovery. AI-powered search has emerged and is drawing more and more people away from traditional search tools, which means the pathways people use to find creators are shifting.

And the shift affects more than just efforts to add more followers. Those in the creator marketplace now must contend with the fact that agencies are increasingly using AI tools to identify creators, while marketers are beginning to build AI visibility into creator briefs and partnership strategies. Adjusting to this shift is important, but experts say the evolution of search behavior won't impact all creators equally.

“How AI search affects creators depends a lot on the type of content and the platform they’re on,” says Max Anderson, Owner and CEO of OnlyFinder, the leading search engine for OnlyFans launched in 2020.

Anderson’s work is focused on creator discovery, ad-tech, digital marketplace economics, consumer behavior, and the data behind how users find and engage with creators online. Through OnlyFinder, a search and discovery platform built around the creator economy, he brings a data-driven perspective on OnlyFans trends, search behavior, monetization, and digital publishing.

“For informational queries, for example, AI is simply a better experience,” Anderson says. “Instead of clicking through 10 blue links and scanning pages for an answer, you ask and get it, and that cannibalizes a very large share of informational search. So if your business is influencer marketing involving informational content, it’s at risk because LLMs will answer those questions directly, and they may or may not cite you. But information retrieval is only one mode of internet behavior.”

Adjusting to how AI search is changing the way people find creators starts with understanding where AI search shines and where it struggles. As Anderson mentions above, AI search is a huge help to those who are looking for information. But analytics derived from recent research show that informational searches account for just over half of the searches people make on Google. And AI search isn’t the best for the other half.

“People go online to shop, comparing options, photos and data side by side, which carries far more commercial value,” Anderson points out. “And they go online to be entertained, to sit back and browse. AI is a much worse experience for both of those.”

The limitations Anderson mentions above suggest creators can avoid being sidelined by being intentional about the way they package their content. Getting direct views, rather than being filtered through AI search results, requires offering experiences that AI isn’t adept at providing.

“The pivot for creators is to offer experiences that don’t make sense inside an LLM interface,” Anderson says. “For example, if you’re providing long-form video that a person actually wants to watch, people will opt for that over an AI-generated synopsis of your video.”

Anderson also points out that the category of content can have an impact on the degree to which creators are affected by AI search. For example, while everyday tasks and academic subjects are core categories for AI search, queries about NSFW topics are often declined.

“If you’re among the nearly 5 million OnlyFans creators, for example, you’re largely unaffected by AI search because, as a matter of policy, the major AI tools won’t answer those questions,” Anderson says. “Ask Google, or a vertical search engine like OnlyFinder, for the best redhead OnlyFans creators, and you get a ranked list of exactly what you wanted. Ask ChatGPT, Claude, or Gemini, and they decline.”

While AI’s effect on finding new followers is important to address, creators also must consider the way it impacts creator partnerships. If companies are now using AI search to find a creator, then creators need to find reliable ways to be included in AI search results.

“An LLM fundamentally predicts the most likely next word based on a huge corpus of internet content used to train it,” Anderson explains. “The more content out there expressing a certain view, the more likely the model is to repeat it. Structured data matters, but what matters most for creators is the quantity of content across many sites. Frequency is what drives success in AI search.”

Anderson recommends that creators looking to show up in AI search build pages on as many platforms as possible, with a consistent name, username, bio, tagline, and photos. Once the pages are established, creators can build their “AI authority” by being repetitive with their messaging.

“If you’re very active on one main platform, use tools to take your content, chop it up, and republish it elsewhere,” Anderson says. “Repetition and breadth of distribution are how you show up more in AI answers, or get them to express the view you’re trying to put into the world.”

Experts are predicting AI will play an increasingly important role in shaping consumer behavior, both by providing a powerful new search pathway and by refining traditional search processes. For creators and influencers who want to remain relevant, adjusting to the new rules of discovery must be a priority. At present, that means taking steps to build AI authority while also offering value that a simple AI overview can’t provide.

This story was distributed as a release by Jon Stojan under HackerNoon’s Business Blogging Program.
